speechtext:
House again in Committee on Bill (No. 88) to provide for the appointment of a Tariff Commission.-Mr. White (Leeds).
On section 4,-matters to be investigated.

Would the Minister of Finance kindly explain the difference between subsection 2 and subsection 4 of section 4? In one case the commission may make certain inquiries under the direction of the minister and in the other when they are authorized to do so by the Governor General in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Both sections are purposely broad and designed to cover matters that have not been particularly specified. Take subsection 2. It is a matter of common experience in the Department of Finance for an application to be made for the lowering or abolition of the duty with regard for instance to certain machinery on the ground that it is not manufactured in Canada and is not likely to be. That is a matter of fact which might very well be referred by the minister to the commission for a report as to the probability of that certain article being manufactured in Canada. Subsection 4 is also designedly broad in its terms. It is fpr the purpose of covering more important matters, for example the chance of increasing trade with certain other countries and the effect that certain tariffs -might have. It is purposely broad so that the commission may be utilized, under the instruction of the Governor General in Council, to report upon matters of that kind.

I think the matter is practically all covered by subsection 1 with the various subsections. I do not see any object in giving the commission the general power in subsection 1 or giving the minister the general power in subsection 2 or giving the Governor General in Council the general power set out in subsection 4.
The minister has informed the House that this is not only to be a permanent tariff board, but, so far as it is possible to make it so, an independent tariff -board. There is no doubt that -he has secured for Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
it a reasonable degree of permanency, for under section 3 of the Bill it is provided that the -commissioners are to be appointed for a definite period of 5 years and cannot be removed except for cause. But I think that the independence of the members of the commission is challenged by every subsection of section 4. The board has no power to initiate anything, no power to take _ a single step without the special instructions of the Minister of Finance or the Governor in Council. I understood, when the Bill was first -brought in that the board, was an independent and permanent board of inquiry, and would be instituted to make, apart from any special instructions from anybody, the inquiries set out in subsection 1 of section 4. But when we come down to analyse the sections of the Bill, we find that the functions of the boiard are subject to the direction of the minister. They cannot enter upon an inquiry, they cannot make a suggestion, they cannot -do any of the things which the Bill contemplates they -should do, and which the public believe they are to do and which are made the main excuse for the introduction of the Bill. Now, I would suggest to the minister that the words in section 4, ' under the direction of the minister,' be struck out. The clause now reads:
4. In, respect o-f goods produced in or imported into Canada the commission shall, under the direction of the minister, make inquiry as to

But why limit it to the minister. Is it not just as has -been predicted in the earlier part of this discussion thiat this commission was designed by the government and tlie Finance Minister to aid its own purposes -and his own purposes in tariff matters, and is not for thie House or the public of Canada at all? Is it -not so that the whole -design and -scope of the Bill i-s to furnish the Finance Minister -and his party with, special information, in disregard- of the rights of the House and of the people in general to receive that information ? To im-y mind, the Bill would be far less objectionable if these words were eliminated as I have -suggested. Though the board must be, and I presume will be under -th-e Bill, established by the government, it should have a certain -amount of independence to be able to inquire here, there or elsewhere without any directions or instructions from the minister. If you give if that power, that freedom of action, it will -have a certain confidence, and, I think it will gain greater respect in the -country than it will otherwise achieve. Now, in passing t-o the concluding words -of subsection 1, I would suggest to the -minister that he also strike out the words ' and report to the minister.' Without such an amendment, see how this plan works out: Here is a board of commii-s-sioiners, -a permanent

and so-called independent board of commissioners who cannot make a move in gaining the information or facts which the government deems it important to know, which cannot even start an investigation without the positive direction of the minister. And when that investigation is completed, the report must be made to tire minister. The matter starts with the minister, and, so far as this clause goes, it ends with the minister. Now, if these facts are essential to he brought out, and if this information is necessary, and we want facts, we want information, the more accurate and fuller that information the better. But where do the members of this House come in; where do the people of the country come in? I am very strongly of opinion that if this commission is to report, it should report to parliament and not to the .minister. It may be beyond the power of members of this House either to get the result of the inquiry or the evidence on which the results are based if the Bill is allowed to go in its present form. It may be that a large fund of information will be available to the minister and his friends, but that surely is not the object of the Bill. It should not be the object, and if it is not, I hope the minister will consent to the elimination of these objectionable words. I ask him in all seriousness if he will consent to strike out the words in subsection 1 of section 4, ' undeT the direction of the minister,' and the concluding words of subsection 1, ' and report to the minister,' and in the latter case, replace the deleted words with ' and report to parliament.' Now, I can understand that if a commission of independent men, men properly selected-not such men as were suggested by my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) but well qualified, independent men -the information gathered by them may be of the greatest benefit to every member of this House. We on this side contend for that. We agree that the government cannot go too far in obtaining accurate and complete information on the subject set out in these subsections; but we do object to these facts being elicited by any secret process and only by special directions. We object to any limitation placed upon the power of the commission to inquire. And I think we are all interested that the report when it is made, and the evidence when it is collected, shall be available, and that the report of the commission shall be a report to the parliament of Canada instead of to the minister. I think that is a businesslike proposition. I make it sincerely, and I hope the minister will give it his serious consideration. It may be necessary, if he does not take that view of it, to move in the matter, but I hope that the suggestion may meet with his approval. I would 'like to hear from him on the subject.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister).
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) that a commission of this kind, and the duties that are allotted to it, must be under the direction of some minister not so far as their methods in making the inquiry are concerned-because in making that inquiry they will be acting independently of any direction from the government-but an inquiry into a particular matter might be more urgent, more insistent in the opinion of those charged with the duties of government than some other matter. Therefore, in view of such considerations it was entirely necessary that a commission of this kind should be under the direction of some department of the government. I would like to remind the hon. gentleman that his own leader, (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) yesterday told us that all this information could be better acquired by appointing statisticians in connection with one of the departments, that of Trade and Commerce, for example. It isi perfectly obvious to my hon. friend, I am sure, that, if he is in accord with the suggestion of his leader, these statisticians would be acquiring information which would be the exact equivalent of the information to be obtained by this commission. With regard to the publicity for which the hon. member is so anxious, the statistics acquired in the manner suggested by the leader of the opposition would be reported to the minister and wrould come down to parliament in the ordinary course. There is nothing more in the provisions of this section than what has been already suggested and' approved by the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition. There is no provision in the Bill for any secrecy, 'except so far as the principle of secrecy has already been applied, by the late government and all preceding governments, with regard to the business affairs of this country. In respect of that provision, the Bill is only carrying out a well recognized principle of the- government. There is no such provision in the Bill as that which my hon. friend suggests.

I take issue with my right hon. friend's explanation of the section, and also with his statement in regard to the position of the right hon. the leader of the opposition. It is one thing to have a statistical bureau or a statistical branch of the Department of Finance under the eye of the minister. That is the proper course, and one which in this instance should have been adopted. That is the well established British way of obtaining statistical information. ' I have heard it stated that the trade statistics of Great Britain are the most convenient and most accurate published by any country in the world. They

are collated and published under the authority of the Board of Trade, the president of which is a member of the Cabinet. Why not adopt the British system in preference to this cheap Yankee device? You could adopt that system simply by establishing, in the Department of Finance or in some other department, a bureau manned with a sufficient staff to collect all this information. In that way you would have the .doctrine of responsibility fully carried out; you would have no independent commission to pass on matters on which thte -minister or the giovennment should pass. What is now proposed is a system modelled in fact upon the United States system. You'appoint a permanent board the members of which are not clerks in any sense of the word. They are commissioners with high standing; you have exalted and dignified them, and you are preparing to pay them handsome salaries; you are giving them very wide and high powers; but these men, an independent board appointed for the purpose of acquiring information, cannot move hand or foot until the Minister of Finance beckons to them what to do; and upon getting the word from him as to how they shall proceed, there is no doubt that they will proceed in accordance with his wishes and those of the government of the day. Why not let this board have powers broad enough to enter upon an inquiry without the direction of anybody? I can understand that cases may arise where information is required speedily. Subsection 2 provides for that, and the minister can get the special information he requires. But all that is contained in subsections ' a ', 'b,' 'c,' 'd,' 'e,' ' f ' and ' g ' should be open to the commissioners, and it should be their duty to enter upon the inquiry and continue it to the end, and make the result of that inquiry public, without instructions from the minister or the government. That is what we are establishing them for, and I think it would improve the Bill very much, in the judgment of the House and the country, if they were given that free hand. They cannot do anything but inquire and report. They have no power to make recommendations or to offer any opinion. We want the information; why not give them a free hand to start in, uncontrolled by the desire of the minister to send them on this expedition or that? The more I look into this Bill the more I realize the almost impossibility of obtaining the information which the government and the House would desire to obtain with regard to facts and conditions as they exist in Canada or elsewhere. Now, ' elsewhere ' is going to be the troublesome part of it. The Board of Tariff Commissioners in the United States have realized that.
They have had the greatest difficulty in foreign countries in getting satisfactory in-Mr. GUTHRIE.
formation, although the United States has a consular system in regard to trade and commercial matters superior to any of the consular systems in the world. In every country, and practically at every port, there has been located a United States consul. The duties of these officers are not so much diplomatic like those of British consular agents. They are to a large extent trade and commercial agents, and one can gain a great deal of information from a persual of the reports of the United States consular agents in Germany, France, Belgium and Holland. I had occasion to go through them two or three years ago in connection with a proposal in regard to technical education, and I found that they dealt almost wholly with trade and commercial matters. The United States consular system is well developed throughout Europe; but, for all that, according to the statement of the Chairman of the United States Tariff Board, they have found the greatest possible difficulty in acquiring accurate information as to conditions, the cost of raw material, wages, transportation and the like in European countries. The Finance Minister is going to be confronted wTith the same difficulty to a much greater extent than have the Tariff Commissioners of the United States. It may be a comparatively easy matter to send representatives to Great Britain and ascertain these facts there; it may be a comparatively easy matter to obtain fairly accurate information in this country. Greater difficulty will be experienced in the United States. There is no power to compel any one in a foreign country to give us this information, and United States manufacturers will not be the easiest men to deal with when the Canadian commissioners seek information from them. But when they go to European countries, where we have no consular agencies, and where we have few trade agencies, 1 believe the difficulties will be almost insurmountable, and the information obtained will be highly inaccurate and thoroughly unreliable. I do not consider that much information of value will be obtained from an investigation in foreign countries; but I do believe that a great deal may be obtained in Canada, in Great Britain, and possibly in the United States, which will be of benefit to us in the future in determining upon our tariff legislation. Now cannot that all be gone into by the Board of Tariff Commissioners without any direction from the minister or the government, or from any other person? It is their duty to do it, they are there for that purpose, and why not let them go ahead, without any special direction, and without limiting their report to the Minister of Finance, but giving it to the public in general?

I think if you examine this clause 4 carefully, you will see that it proceeds from the lesser to the greater, that the first and second paragraph are more narrow, and more definite, and more specific than the 3rd and 4th paragraphs, and that the 5th paragraph really refers wholly to clause 4. Now let us see just how this works out in principle. Who is it that brings a Tariff Bill into this House, that presents the case for the revision of our tariff? It is the Minister of Finance. Clause 1 and clause 2 naturally give to the Minister of Finance the power of direction over that body of experts, that will collect for him the facts and information which he will need in order to make his draft Bill relating to the tariff, which draft Bill, I have no doubt, he submits to his colleagues which his colleagues, when satisfied with it, as a government, submit to the House. Therefore, whether we express it in the Bill or not, it will be the Finance Minister who will have the general charge and direction over that Tariff Commission, and it will be through the Finance Minister that that commission makes its report to the Cabinet and through the Cabinet to parliament. We may or may not specifically state in the Bill that it shall be under the direction and control of the Finance Minister, but whether we do that or not, that will actually be the case.
Why not say that the commission is independent?

Now, as to making the commission independent, I think that hon. members will see that if there is anything that will lead to confusion and general dislocation, it is that proposition made by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). This Tariff Commission, if they are to accomplish anything, will have to take up the work in a regular and definite way, and naturally the way that they will go about it, is to take up in order such schedules in the tariff, as in the judgment of the government call for first and earliest attention. Now there is no other body but the government of the country who can take upon themselves the authority to say that the wool schedule, for instance, or the iron schedule, or the cotton schedule shall first occupy the attention "of this commission.
That is provided for by subsection 2.

Therefore, I say it will be necessary for the government to say to the commission, we desire that an inquiry shall first be directed upon such and such schedules, and surely through no one but the Finance Minister will these commands actually be given to the Tariff Commission, and when they prepare their report, whether it is stated so in specific words or not, it will be actually made to the Finance Minister and through the Finance Minister to the government.

If the hon. gentleman will read subsection 2, would not that meet the very objection he is urging to my argument? That gives the Finance Minister the power, when he desires to bring in a tariff, to investigate certain things. But I want to point out this contingency: Suppose there is a demand on the part of the public to have a certain industry investigated, for instance, the shoe manufacturing industry, and the Finance Minister does not think it should be investigated. Should not the Tariff Commission of their own motion, be entitled to go into that questioh, under subsection 2?

If anything is to be accomplished by this Tariff Commission in the way of gradually accumulating a library of facts and definite information that will serve as a basis, not only for the first tariff Bill, but for all subsequent tariff measures, they must proceed in an orderly manner. Naturally there will be but one authority to which applications for dealing with specific subjects will be made, and that is the government, and naturally there must be some special commission that will determine in the various claims which are made which claim is the most urgent and of' the most immediate importance. Somebody has to take the responsibility of saying to that commission; You will study such and such subject first, and such and such subjects next, and you will report to us from time to time as you complete your inquiries in these various categories, and then we shall determine what action to take, and as to whether that action shall be immediate or deferred. You will surely get into confusion if you sit here and say to them, Go away, start on any subject you like, take your own time, study any subject you please, and report at any time you please, and we in the meantime will go cn with cur business. This government will have to decide on what subjects they consider tariff legislation is of most urgent importance. Thei'efore, they will say to that commission:	Devote your energies first to such
and such a subject, and when you have dealt with that, go on with the other schedules. I think I am right in saying that in the course of two or three years every item in our tariff schedules, we may' reasonably expect, will be submitted to the consideration of this commission, they will send in probably a dozen volumes of reports in due course to the govern-ernment, and in due course these reports will reach this parliament; but the order

they will take will have to be determined by the government, and through the Finance Minister indicated to this Tariff Commission. Now clauses 1 and 2 deal with a limited, definite and narrow sphere of activity, in which the order would be determined by the Minister of Finance. Clauses 3 and 4 are much wider, they are of a general character, and in 3 and 4 the indication comes from the Governor in Council, and probably the report will be made to the Cabinet direct. Those are matters somewhat out of the routine, not a consecutive investigation of tariff schedules. Number 3, I think, relates to combines, 4 relates to trade treaties, and those, as they from time to time come before the House and require attention, will be referred to the commission only when the government think it is of sufficient imoortance to interrupt them in their regular work, and ask them to take up these special subjects from time to time as they arise.
Now, as to foreign countries, the hon. gentleman suggests that we shall be able to obtain no information in foreign countries. In the first place, let me point out that the United States is having no difficulty in getting information from a great many sources. That information can be obtained by us through consular assistance, we can get it through the assistance of the British Embassy. Further than that there is no reason why we should not avail ourselves of some of the information that has been acquired by other commissions of investigation; we will not be above taking advantage of any investigations that the American Tariff Commission have carried on abroad, which, in the opinion of our commissioners, will be of use to this government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Assuming that the government wishes to formulate a policy when parliament is not sitting, and that the information has already been collected by the board, to whom should the board report in order that the government might formulate its policy?
Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER. The commission will report to parliament, the government will formulate its policy upon it, and I shall have, like anybody else, as a member of parliament, the right to criticise the action taken by the government. What I contend is, that if you are to depart from the principle which has been adopted elsewhere, of having information of this character collected under ministerial responsibility by a statistical bureau, then the commission must be under the direct control of parliament. It should not be possible for the government to interfere with its work. If the government, as was suggested a moment ago by the hon. member for St. Antoine, wanted to have some particular information upon some point, the minister, under section 2, could say:	I
. want a special report upon this or that point. If somebody comes to parliament and asks to have some matter investigated if somebody comes, as was suggested by the minister a moment ago, and asks for a duty upon such an article, or the removal of the duty upon another article, and it becomes a question whether or not that article is manufactured in Canada, the minister may refer the matter to the commission, and get the information in that way. If the Governor in Council wants to have some information upon some other matter, then again, he can apply to the commission. What I suggest to my hon. friends is, that if they want to be consistent in this matter, and if we are to have all we expect to have from this commission and the work that is intended to be done
by it, and which is enumerated in clause 4, the commission should not be subject to interference by the minister. The commission should be primarily responsible to parliament. I repeat that this does not prevent the minister or the Governor-in-Council, if they want to have special information upon any matter, from applying to the commission, and securing that information, but I feel very strongly that if we are to have this commission as it is intended, and as we always understood it to be, an independent commission, it should not be liable to be controlled by the-I will not say caprice,-but by the authority of the minister. It should be under the control of parliament and of (parliament alone, primarily. My hon. friend to use his own words, states that this commission should be composed of the biggest men the country can give us. Does he believe that, if we have a commission composed of the most eminent business men of the city of Montreal, they will be satisfied to be treated as clerks, under the Department of Finance or the Department of Trade and Commerce? Is it not better, if we are to have the benefit of their business ability, training and knowledge, that they should go on untrammelled and prepare for the next session of parliament a report on these important subjects which are enumerated in section 4?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has returned to the question of whether it is advisable to have a bureau or a Tariff Commission. One would think that the idea of a Tariff Commission had never come to the mind of my right hon. friend before. I desire to call the attention of the House to the report of a speech which my right hon. friend delivered in the City of Montreal in October, 1908, on which occasion Ire was the honoured guest of the Canadian Manufacturers' (Association, about, which we have heard so much during the last two days. I intend to read some extracts from what he is reported to have said. Discussing the woollen tariff he said:
As you know-you have referred to it, it has been part of your debates-you approached the government during the last session to have an increase in the woollen duties, and I will preface whatever remarks I may have to offer now by the fact that I was not a member of the Tariff Commission which prepared the tariff which was adopted in 1907.
That was a commission or committee of ministers.
The members of the commission were my colleagues, Mr. Fielding, the Minister of Finance, Sir Richard Cartwright, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Paterson, the Minister of Customs and Mr. Brodeur, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
When they brought in their report, and when they embodied it in the form of the

Act of 1907, I think it was pretty generally accepted at that "time that they had reached about a happy medium, and taking it all in all, that the tariff was fairly satisfactory. But it so happened that in the course of a few months, the woollen industry, which it must be admitted has not been flourishing very much for the last few years, became embarrassed and was brought into very serious difficulties. Then we were approached to make some concessions to increase the duties.
I understood the right hon. gentleman to say yesterday that he was a free trader, or that he believed in tariff for revenue only, and if I am under a wrong impression as to that I would like to be corrected now. Well, at this time, the right hon. gentleman had been asked to consider the question of the tariff duties with regard to the woollen schedule, and he said to his audience further on in his speech:
Why is it that you cannot produce what is produced hy the British manufacturer? Well, Sir, if it be that the conscience of the Canadian manufacturer is too severe, that they will give only pure wool and nothing else, I say that is not business. I tell you I am not a business man, but the first rule of the business man is to give to his customer what lie wants to buy. And if that be true, why is it that you do not give him that cloth which he wants to buy? That is the reason and it seems to me to be a very strong argument. This was the answer which was given to me upon the very anxious inquiries which I made -the answer that was given to me was this -the British manufacturer can produce the cheap article of cloth from East India wool and from cheap waste which he gets at a price which the Canadian manufacturer cannot have. Well, Sir, that is a satisfactory answer, so far as I am concerned.
I am sorry my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) is not here; yesterday he said the end of production was consumption and I set out that doctrine of the hon. member for Red Deer against the statement- of the right hon. the leader of the opposition when he says that, so far as he is concerned, the answer is satisfactory :	v
If it he true that the Canadian consumer wants that cloth, if it he true that the British manufacturer can have the raw material of that cloth cheaper than the Canadian manufacturer can have it in Canada, that is a condition of things which is in itself one to be considered, and which cannot be overlooked.
Why cannot it be overlooked; what is wrong about the British manufacturer obtaining this raw material more cheaply than the Canadian manufacturer; if there is anything in the theory advanced yesterday by my right hon. friend, where is he concerned in the cost of the raw material to the British manufacturer? I say that this statement here does not square with the policy laid down by the right hon.

-in the conversation I had with my friend the Minister of Customs, when I told him that we must do something, or look into this case and see whether or not something should he or should not be done, he suggested himself that we should send at once a commissioner to England

My right hon. friend seems to suspect his own government because, remember, it was his own government that was to appoint this commission. He seems to have it in his mind, it was an impression probably based on past- experience, that there might be a party heeler on his commission and so he announces twice that there should not be a party heeler, and them he says:
Not a politician.
He is afraid also of politicians. The right hon. gentleman's own experience leads him to believe that there must necessarily be a party heeler or a politician on his commission, and from what lias been said by him it would seem to me there was reason for suspicion that possibly, in spite of his best intentions there might be on his commission a party heeler or a politician. Well, let me assure my hon. friend the leader o-f the opposition, that the same conditions will not obtain with this government as appear to have obtained formerly in that regard. He himself suggested in his speech that we should at once send a commissioner to England, not a party heeler, not -a politician, 'but a business man, an expert, just what we are contending for in this commission; a commission of experts, of business mien, of capable men, to obtain information upon which we may act rationally in connection with tariff 'matters. That is just what my right lion.' friend was aspiring to, only he did not carry it out as we propose to carry it out. The right hon. gentleman continued:
-not a party heeler, not. a politician, hut a , business man, an expert, and I have reason to believe, though I have not spoken to Mr. I'aterson since this expert has already been sent by him to England, and he is now doing the work. (Applause.)
That statement was followed with applause, as no doubt we would expect to have such -a statement followed with applause, when made by my right hon. and eloquent friend. He continues to say;
Gentlemen, I am not here to say that your demand is just or unjust; I am not here to say that your request is fair or unfair, that it is right or not right

Here, he is not in a position to pronounce, because he has not the facts. He continues:
-hut I am here to say that your complaints are such that they are entitled to the fullest consideration on the part of the Canadian government. We have not been willing up to the present time to disturb the tariff; it is only 24 months old, not even so yet; and therefore, if we are to have a principle of stability about the tariff we should proceed very leisurely upon all such inquiries. But at all

events there is a grave condition of things and we are prepared to meet it and to meet it in the manner which I have suggested.
And the manner be has suggested is, by appointing a commission to obtain the tacts upon which the government might act, and that is precisely the principle that is embodied in this Bill.
I hope that this will command the assent of every reasonable man, as you are all reasonable men at this hoard.
Now, if that commanded and should command the assent of every reasonable man, why is it unreasonable that we should appoint a Tariff Commission by this Bill to do precisely the same work as that which my right hon. friend has in view, and with precisely the same object, namely, that we might have information on which we can construct a rational tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was a splendid speech It is a lesson and a model, and I am only sorry that my right hon. friend has retrograded from the principles he laid down in that speech. It is one of the best arguments that I have run across for the appointment of a Tariff Commission, because it is based upon the desire of my right hon. friend for facts at a time when the question was up for his decision. My right hon. friend goes further, and talks of a permanent Tariff Commission. I wish to be fair to my right hon. friend: I do not . say that the commission of which he appeared to approve was precisely on all-fours with this proposed commission; but I am going to show from what he said that the principle of obtaining through a commission information on which the government would act is by no means a departure from the policy which he himself has laid down in the past. He said further:
There is just another idea as to which I want to have a word of expression. You have stated, Mr. Chairman, in your address that you desire to have a permanent Tariff Commission.
I must believe that my hon. friend was sincere in his address to this association, and was not merely flirting with them politically. He said:
I do not exactly realize yet what is meant by a permanent Tariff Commission; but I am free to say that if it be meant that you would have a permanent commission such as I think they have in the United States

What about that cheap Yankee device which we heard about from the hon. member for South Wellington?
Mr. WHITE (Leeds'
-to follow the workings of the tariff from day to day, to follow the incidents, to follow the effects upon the producers and the consumer, and its daily effects upon the community, I do not see any reason why such a commission should not be appointed.
My right hon. friend and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association were evidently in perfect accord after that historic dinner, which took place in October, 1908. How far he has modified his views since, and how consistent he is in his modification of such views, I leave this House to judge. A little further on he said this:
I must be careful.
What lie has said lie has said carefully, and I think he said a good deal. If ne had not in mind that he must be careful,
I do not know how much further he would have gone. He went on:
You know parliament was dissolved yesterday and we are in the heat of an election now. My second is Mr. Monk, a prominent member of the opposition, and I must not make any promises, because I don't know what will be the consequences. I make no promises, but I say the matter will be looked into very carefully by my associates any myself.
With regard to what the right hon. leader of the opposition, and the hon. member for * South Wellington have said with regard to the members of the commission being treated as clerks, either they have entirely misconceived the purpose of this Bill, which I can hardly believe possible in view of the explanations which have been given, or they are continuing to read into this Bill something that does not and never did exist in it. Now, what is the principle of the Bill? Hon. gentlemen talk about a Tariff Commission independent of the government. The principle of this Bill is this, and it cannot be anything else under our constitutional system: The government is responsible for the tariff, and that responsibility cannot be devolved upon an outside body. This commission is a body ancillary to the government, directed by the government to accomplish certain purposes, namely, to give us the information that we need in framing a rational tariff. The expression ' under the direction of the minister means simply this, that instead of letting a commission, who are not directly responsible to the people, as the government is, pursue any desultory investigation they desire, they must be under the control or direction of the minister, who must know what matter is more urgent than others.
Is not that provided for in subsection 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it is not. The first clauses are general clauses. To say that a commission might start out and pur-

sue its investigation into anything here, there or elsewhere, would be simply to destroy the very purpose of a- commission, which is to accomplish results, to bring about efficiency, to give us the information that we need from time to time in order to frame our tariff rates, and in order to remedy defects in the tariff as they become known, and the minister, informed by public opinion in many ways, realizes that there are certain things that must be investigated before anything else, and he is responsible. This only means that the minister must give the commission direction as to the lines of inquiry it is to pursue in order that it may be'a useful part of the machinery of government for obtaining the information desired.
My hon. friend evidently has the conception that this should be an independent commission roving at its own sweet will in a desultory fashion about the country, not directed in any way, not responsible to the government, and bringing down reports and handing them to parliament. My hon. friend spoke about subverting the principles of the constitution. If the Bill were drawn along the line he suggests it would go very far to justify that criticism. The (purpose of the Bill is to enable the government primarily responsible, to obtain information upon which it might first make up its mind as to tariff changes and then bring them down to this House. As I have said, the information is departmental, it is contained in reports to the department and as such as subject to the orders of the House as is other departmental information. Let us assume that instead of a Tariff Commission, we had a bureau of statistics. A great deal of information would be acquired from time to time by that bureau. Does any hon. gentleman mean to say that if this House asked that the information accumulated by the bureau should be brought down, it would not be produced? It is preposterous, of course, it would be' brought down. There is no difference in kind between the information accumulated by the Tariff Commission and that which would be accumulated by such a bureau, as my hon. friend has referred to, it would be precisely the same kind of information obtained in one case by a tribunal and in the other by a sub-department of the finance department, by clerks or experts as my hon. friend has said. That being the case, all the arguments that have been brought forward by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) must fail of their effect.
Subsection 2 refers to other matters, as for example whether Canada is able or likely to manufacture certain commodities. This commission should in time, become skilled with regard to matters of this kind. What are the resources of Canada with regard to raw material, what would be the
effect of a certain change in tariff, anything that, as a matter of fact, relates to the tariff or is connected with its administration and not included in the preceding sections may, by virtue of that subsection, be referred by the minister to the commission for inquiry and report. Subsection 4 has been made very wide indeed to cover matters not specifically covered by the preceding subsections. I think the objections raised are fanciful, they disappear when we come to examine them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What we are discussing at this moment is what should be the character of the commission which parliament is now creating, should it be an independent commission or a commission ancillary to the government. My hon. friend (Mr. White), has endeavoured to fortify himself by opinions expressed in 1908 during a debate in which I discussed two questions, one of them being the woollen duties. I then said that I had no objection whatever to sending a special commission to Great Britain and Germany to investigate the matter. That is done by all governments at all times: The government have power now to appoint men for the very puupose of obtaining information upon certain matters. There was nothing extraordinary about my suggestion, but that is no precedent for what we are doing now. My hon. friend would have found something more to the point in the other part of my speech, in which I said that we might consider the advisability of having such a commission, as they then had in the United States. That was considered perhaps too ambitious. There was then in the United States no such commission as has been appointed by President Taft, they had something very much in the nature of a bureau of statistics that collected very valuable information upon prices, methods of production, Taw material &c., and I thought at the time that we might very well create a similar bureau. But this idea has been discarded, my hon. friend is not to-day introducing legislation to provide for such a commission as they had at that time, he is copying rather what has been done since under the administration of President Taft, he is really copying the Bill introduced in Congress, but not yet passed. We have discarded the idea I then had of having a commission ancillary to the government, a branch of the administration and we are appointing a broad and wide and big commission. The impression has been created in the public mind since the introduction of this Bill that my hon. friend is creating a very broad and independent commission. The commission ought to be one thing or the other, it ought to be an ancillary commission or rather a statistical bureau such as we have designed, under his own control,

or else a parliamentary commission primarily responsible to parliament. What is the objection of my hon. friend to this? He said that an independent commission could go at its own sweet will and do anything it pleased. I beg to differ from him. This commission could not go at its own sweet will, it would have to do what it was enjoined to do, to collect intormation on this, that and the other subject, upon the cost of production, upon raw materials, upon transportation, upon methods of manufacture, upon prices, and bring that information before parliament. That would be the first thing to be done, such a commission could not go out at its own sweet wili but would have to fulfil the duty imposed on it by parliament. My hon. friend in another part of the Bill very properly reserves to himself the power to impose certain work upon the commission and he reserves to the Governor in Council also the power to impose certain other work upon the commission. To say that under such circumstances the commission should be simply under the jurisdiction of the minister is not in accordance with the conception of the feature of the commission which would give it its greatest usefulness, that is that it should be an independent commission. The present government have appointed several commissions to deal with different subjects. These commissioners have been given certain powers, they have been instructed to do certain work. Does the minister believe now that it would be possible for the Governor in Council to go back to these commissioners, and say: You shall do your work in such and such a manner. Such a course is inconceivable. This is the same thing, this should be above all things a parliamentary commission, of course with power to the government to use it when they think it advisable to do so.

In the creation of this commission and of previous commissions, I think we are taking rather the wrong method. We should not spend too much time here in discussing what the powers of the commissioners are to be, we should rather follow the example of the United States where the special commissioners are placed under the direction of the President or with us it would be under the general direction of the government. The Bills creating these commissions should riot go into details as does the Bill creating the Grain Commission.
But the responsibility should be on the government of directing the commission. The government having full responsibility, ought, in each case, to define the reference made to the commission. In that way, you would reach an ascertainment of the facts and a realization of the object of Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
the commission, far better than by detailed definition with regard to the commission under an Act of parliament. Rather than maintain the policy that we appear to have adopted here, I would see the powers of the commission made very general, the whole placed under the direction of some responsible minister, and then hold the government to responsibility. And the government ought to assume that responsibility and define the reference in every case. In the case of the Railway Commission, the work to be done is different. In that case you have to be more definite in outlining the powers to be exercised. But in the case of commissions of this kind which, as has been said here, are ancillary to the government, the definition ought to be broad and general, and the responsibility ought to be on the government. There will be cases that cannot be reached, even with all the care that we can exercise. My view with regard to these commissions is that we must have more of them, and that we are going to have more of them.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Government by commission.

Yes, I have no doubt that there will be more and more government by commission, but with it should go more and more responsibility on the part of the government for the work of the commission. What I wish to keep clear is the absolute responsibility of the government to the people. That secured, I am not so much concerned about the details. Our Statute-book is getting too large; we are taking up too much of our time with all these details. 1 contend that you would get a better administration ar.d a better investigation if you maintain clearly the responsibility of the government. It may be that after a while a commission of this kind will build up a practice and will have rules that will have the effect of law. The cou-ts that we have created, while they administer the law, have made rules that are particularly a part of the law, and that are observed and respected by every one. That is what we want to get into our commissions; we want to get a flexibility and yet an effectiveness that will be equal to the occasion, and this cannot be attained with too much limitation and definition. Create a commission with broad powers and under a responsible head-as they say in the United States, ' under the direction of the President.' 1 regretted to hear the discussion of details here in the matter of the Grain Commission. I would rather see a law creating a Grain Commission under the direction of the government to deal with

the grain trade of the country. I am not so much dissatisfied with the Bill now before us, but rather object to the discussions here of limitations in connection with the commission.
Sir \YILFRID LAURIER. That sort of doctrine would well have suited Charles I.

I am not talking the.doctrire of Charles 1, but the doctrine of responsibility to the people. And the way to maintain an effective responsibility is to give broad powers and then hold those to whom they are given responsible for the exercise of those powers. If you have that as you ought to have it, in this commission, something will be done.
What little study of the tariff I have made leads me to believe that the facts can be ascertained by some kind of inquiry, and that men outside of parliament, men authorized to do it, will get thost facts, will analyse them and present them. And these men will be a board or court where those who wish to be heard can be heard, and all the facts presented. That will relieve parliament. We are talking of parliament being overworked. If the threshing out of facts can take plaee outside of parliament, and if we can get a statement for the guidance of parliament, it will facilitate the work of parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Or dispense with it,
No, facilitate it. I know of nobody who did so much to take away the responsibility of government and the rights of parliament, as did the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) himself.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I would like to say a word; and first, to express a little faint surprise at the position taken ky. the right hon. leader of the opposition (bir Wilfrid Laurier) which I have heard here for the first time, not having had the pleasure of hearing him ithe other afternoon. I think it will help us in parliament and in the country as well to look a little at the genesis of this commission. What has given rise to the talk about a commission, and to the idea that such an instrumentality as the commission was necessary? It arose out of the practical difficulties met in obtaining information for tariff legislation and out of the general impression, not only with the ministers themselves, who had to gather information, but with almost every interest in the country, that the information gathered was fragmentary and was not in its width or accuracy information upon which a tariff should be based. Sometimes the committee of ministers that went around the country were referred to as the ' Tariff Commission. ' They were a tariff commission in no sense at all. They were a commission in. no sense at all. They were simply three or four gentlemen who having gone about certain portions of the country hearing people giving their various views for and against different phases of a tariff measure, tariff proposals, tariff wishes and wants, made up their minds as best they could.
But I think I am not violating any confidence, when I say, as a member of one of those so-called commissions, or better, committees of parliament, it was never satisfactory, and never resulted in what was intended. In fact, the ministers themselves, passing to and fro through the country, listening for an hour to-day end-an hour to-morrow to the divergent and different views, almost always sketchy, ended by having a more hazy idea than probably they had when they started out.
I went over this country from one end of it to the other, holding, in connection with my colleagues, open meetings, where everybody was welcome, and where we listened to what the people had to say. It resulted in this, that mostly you heard long-winded statements made by people who were fond



of talking, and generally people who had some particular fads to air. You could not turn them down, you were a committee of ministers, and the public was invited, and you had to listen to them courteously. You got another kind of information. You had carefully prepared expert statements by those who were advocating a certain interest, who came there to advocate a certain side of it, who would not look at arguments on the other side, who made as completely an ex parte case as they possibly could, and added to it their figures and their statements; a bulky document was filed away by your secretary, and taken along with you for the rest of the trip. Now, after that had gone on for one, two, or three months, or more, the ministers. came together to frame a tariff. What had they ? A lot more or less hazy impressions, where one blended with the other to such an extent that you scarcely had any clear idea of any one phase of the question; bundles, and bundles, and bundles of documents and statements, which you never afterwards looked at, which you were not able to digest, and which, when parliament called for them, were stacked up on the table so numerous that any man who looked at the outside of the package never thought of going into them. You had long statements, but no digestion or analysis of those statements. The ministers themselves were not able to digest or analyse those statements, the secretaries were not able to do it. It required expert men who understood that kind of thing, who made it their study, and had gone over them, had gone to the very bottom of them, and had added to the knowledge of them, knowledge gained otherwise, to make any fair analysis. I put it to my right hon. friend, and if his late Minister of Finance or his Minister of Customs were here, I would put it to them, whether what I am saying with reference to the modus operandi is not absolutely true. As a matter of fact, in the olden times my colleagues and myself came and sat down in the hurly burly of an approaching or a continuing session, hearing everybody; without having time to make investigation and making a more or less rule -of thumb tariff. Hoping that we might do what was the best in the main but hardly ever sure, and basing it upon no careful analysis of the conditions. I do not doubt for a moment, that if Mr. Fielding were here, he would rise in his rplace and say that his experience was much like mine. Out of that, the ministers began to feel, and the people of this country, especially the business interests, began to feel, that there was a better way to get at the basis of a tariff, namely to choose men whose whole business it should be, not to make schedules, not to lay down percentages, not in any sense to Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
recommend that this should be protected or that should be protected, not to tell you that you ought to have a tariff here and you ought to have a certain tariff there, not to intimate to you what protection they thought was necessary in this case or that case; but men whose sole business and duty it was to get at the whole facts of the case, and place those facts before the government, before parliament and before the people at large. You say sometimes that this is to relieve the government. It is a very -poor idea of it, that, if you say^ it is to relieve members of parliament, it is a very poor idea of it, that. The business of making tariffs will be just the hardest, and most delicate, and responsible business, when you have a basis of facts that a good commission has gathered, that it has ever been in this country. No minister or -ministry will hereafter be able to shield themselves behind generalities. Parliament itself will be put in possession of every fact that the ministers possess; every one of the 220 members of parliament will be an efficient check upon the ministerial quota that are laying before them what they propo-se to do in the matter of the tariff, -and in the matter of charges. They will be able to judge. Heretofore a minister has been able to escape behind generalities, he has been able to shield himself behind the ignorance of parliament with reference to the real conditions of every item upon which it was desired to act. After this, if this commission is rightly appointed, and if it rightly does its duty, not only the members will be judging the ministers, not only will the ministers be put on their mettle, because they have got to come to the touchstone of facts, but the intelligent country outside will have a chance of judging of a tariff such as it never had before.
Is it my hon. friend's idea that these reports will be brought down to parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I never had the least idea that they would not,
Is there any objection to making the Bill definite in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: All these reports given in the line of what is called for, in getting information which is the basis of tariff measures, is the property, not only of the government, or of the minister, but of parliament and of the country. Nobody, I think in this House, has ever had any other idea of it.
The Minister of Finance distinctly stated that yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think we elaborated this matter in council. So far as I am concerned, I never had any

other idea of it than that. So I say that that will be the position of things. No one will be able to shield himself behind an ex parte statement, or behind lack of knowledge when the knowledge will be there, and every intelligent man will be able to draw his own conclusions.
Now I consider this to be another great effect of a Tariff Commission of this kin/d. A (basis of facts is what we want to get at It is invaluable for the legislator, it is invaluable for the minister who is framing a tariff, it is invaluable for the business man; it is invaluable in this respect, that it prepares and puts before the country a touchstone where competent and incompetent men meet, as it were, on common ground, when grievances are raised or are alleged. To-day men honestly think that the tax upon agricultural implements is too high, that the men who are making them are making fortunes, and that this tax ought to be lowered.
They get the best information they can and they cite that information as a proof that their assertion is right. The man who is making implements, knowing, perhaps a little more about the modus operandi and. about the business itself, combats the farmer and says: No, you are wrong in your information; it i3 thus and so. Both of these are ex parte statements, whatever else you may say about them. The farmer never wants to get rid of any fair proportion of taxes that he ought to contribute to the government and upkeep of this country. The farmer is willing to pay his proper proportion of taxes, but he wants to know that he is not paying more than his proper proportion of taxes. He does not want to shirk his taxes, neither does any other good citizen of this country. Now, in a dispute like that, is it not invaluable to have the absolute facts, as near as you can ascertain them by a commission or a committee of men, whose duty it is to get at the facts, who become skilful in getting facts and skilful in1 placing them in the way in which they can be most easily read and understood? Surely it is the touchstone to the farmer and the agricultural implement maker and their grievance is settled by reference to a standard of fact. But, if it is proved that, taking into account the whole business, its costs and charges; the tariff is too great upon that article, down it comes and no ministry can keep it up, because it is shown by the facts and the ministry could not find sup- ; port in parliament unless they were right 5 in that matter. Show that and it comes [DOT] down. Show the opposite and every fair- i minded_ man who believes in keeping the * industries of Canada intact, will surely say, i if it is not enough, let a little more be : added. But no commission dare say * whether it shall be lowered or whether it -94$
shall be heightened, whether it shall be 17 per cent, or 25 per cent, or 10 per cent. It is not their business .and they go outside of their business entirely when they attempt to do anything like that.
In addition to that, such a commission must have some directive power. It must have guidance. Who shall guide it? Shall parliament guide the commission ? You could not have a more bulky unmanageable guide than parliament to guide the commission. Parliament cannot discipline itself, cannot agree within itself; it is actuated by two entirely different ideas. The only way you can have correct guidance for a commission of this kind is by a committee of parliament which is responsible to parliament and responsible for its guidance of this commission. Why all these fanciful views as to what the government purpose to do or as to what will be done by this commission ? The government cannot shield themselves behind incorrect or wrong methods or methods which are not thorough in regard to this matter. Your commission is moving through the country in the sight of the world and of parliament, its results come-to parliament through the report which has been made to the minister. No ministry could successfully delegate their work to .a commission.
But remember that the minister is a politician. He is a Tory; he is a Grit; that is a fact, but there is neither Toryism nor Gritism in absolute facts, and this commission is told to go and get absolute facts A commissioner may be a Tory when he starts or a Grit when he starts, a protectionist when he .starts or a free trader when he starts-, but when he comes to the cost of cotton everybody knows that there is neither Toryism nor Gritism in determining the cost of cotton or wool, or leather, or the cost of the processes which are put upon them. Toryism or Gritism, free trade or protection, will have nothing to do with the matter; yet, you know that the men who get the results of the investigations of the commission will go to work and place upon these articles a tariff of so much per cent here and so much per cent there. It will be so whether they are protectionists, whether they are tariff reform men or whether they are free traders. This seems to me to be the simplest thing in the world.	I do not want to give mv
hon. friends advice; they are older in experience and certainly older in wickedness than I am; they do not need any advice from me, .but my wonder is that they have taken up .this position of absolute opposition to getting the facts. Liberals are not supposed to fear the facts. The time w-as in the years not long gone toy when we tried to lift the lid,, but the lid

Mr. Chairman, 1 only want to make a very few remarks on this important question and if I did not feel my responsibility in connection with the people that I have the honour to represent I would not perhaps trouble the committee at all. My right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) came west last fall and made the declaration that he would give the people a Tariff Commission. The more I have heard this question discussed in the House and the more I have thought over it, the more convinced I am that we aTe going to solve the problem of distrust between the two great divisions int-o which we might say the citizens of this country are divided. We can almost say that these two divisions are composed of the manufacturers on the one side and the agricultural -class on the other. So far as my experience goes, I think I can say without fear of contradiction that there has been for a great many years a feeling of distrust, of want of confidence, between these two great classes of citizens. Speaking for the west, I think I can say that we are almost tired and weary of the word * tariff.'

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Since I came to this House, the tariff has been a fpotent factor in our discussions. We read in history that one of the queens of England said that after her death the word ' Calais ' would be found written on her heart, and I believe. Sir, that if a post-mortem is ever. held on the members who have been sitting in this House for several years past, the word ' Tariff ' will be found written in their hearts. And, why is it that we have been so long in coming to a practical conclusion in connection with this great question. 1 have said that I believe there is distrust . and want of confidence between the manufacturing and the -agricultural classes in this country, and, personally I believe, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, that that feeling has arisen simply because we fail to understand each other as is the case with regard to other questions which engage the attention of the people of this country. We in the west think we pay too much for our agricultural implements j I am mighty sure that the farmers in my constituency think so, at any rate. The manufacturers of Canada say, I suppose, that we are not paying too much, and who knows? I do not know, and one of the duties of this commission will be to find out. If we have the right kind of a commission, and I aim strong on that point of having the right kind of a commission, one of the utilities of that commission will be that they will give us such definite, such fair, and such independent information that you can place it before the farmers or any other class of the community and allow them to judge for themselves whether they are paying too much, or whether the manufacturer is asking too much. I have always listened with a great deal of pleasure and interest to the remarks of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) but I never heard him labour so, as he did the other day in this House, when he was trying to read into this Bill something which it absolutely does not contain. I say, Sir, if it contains what he and other hon. gentlemen opposite say it contains, I am opposed to it, and I go-further and I say that if it contains all that was read into it by my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) I am also opposed to it. The great question is: who is this commission to serve. Hon. gentlemen opposite say it is going to serve the manufacturers.
Hear hear.

Hon. gentlemen opposite say: 'Hear, hear,' to that, but my belief is" that it is intended to serve all classes of the community, and that is the kind of commission I want, and if we are honest about it, that is the kind of commission it will be. Once this Bill passes, then the most important question is as to

the personnel of this eommision. The Minister of Finance told us that no man would be appointed because of his occupation, and while that was a good thought, I would like if he had gone a little further, and said that no man would be kept off the commission because of his occupation. We want broad, big men on this commission, and, if the commission is going to do what I believe it can do, and what I hope, it will do, then we must have at least one member of it, whose environment has been amongst the great agricultural classes of this country. I believe that the men appointed on that commission will be fair, and will try to be fair-, but in order that we may get out of that commission all there is in it for the . best interest of Canada, we must have some man who understands the great agricultural classes of the community, and who is in sympathy with them. Now, as to whose charge this commission should be under. I have something to say, and there is no doubt that there must be somebody to run it, and by that, I do not mean to say that it is a machine.
I am afraid it is.

I know my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff), is very suspicious, but I say to him that if we are to act in the best interests of all the people of Canada, _ we must get out of our minds this suspicion, and deal with the question fairly and squarely, as it presents itself to us.
^ Mr. TURRIFF. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Schaffner) has himself expressed more suspicion than any * gentleman who has yet spoken on the Bill.

All right, if you believe so, but I am saying what I think. Of course, this commission comes very properly and very logically under the Minister of Finance, who has to do with tariff matters. The ^Minister of Finance must direct the commission, but, when I say that, I do not mean to be understood as saying that when this commission goes out to investigate any particular industry, the Minister of Finance is to direct the commission what to do. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance, if he goes that far, and' if he does, I am opposed to it. Supposing, for example, the farming industry of this country comes to the conclusion that something in connection with the tariff is bearing on them too heavily, and believes that it should be investigated, I do not take it that the Minister of Finance could or would prevent this class of the community from having this investigation into what they want to have investigated. I do not think he goes that far.
The Bill goes that far.

I do not believe it does. The Bill says that the commission shall be under the direction of the Minister of Finance, but what part of the Bill goes any further than that?
Mr. OLIVER, Subclause 4 of section 4.
Mr. SCHAFFNER, What tjhat clause says is this:
It shall also be the duty of the commission to inquire into any other matter or thing in relation to the trade or commerce of Canada, which the Governor in Council sees fit to refer to the commission for inquiry or report.
Is that what the hon. gentleman refers to?
Suppose the minister does not direct, what happens then? We want to give the commission power to investigate that without the minister.

I am not very familiar with responsible government; but it seems to me that the strongest point in favour of this commission is that it will remove the distrust to which _ I refer. While I am quite willing that the minister should direct the matter, I think that the agriculturists of this country who form a large proportion of the population, should be able to go to him and ask him to investigate any matter that they think should be investigated. I think that is a fair proposition, and I cannot think that the Minister of Finance would refuse such a request, whether it is provided for in the Bill or not. The whole object of this Bill, as I understand it, is to get information.
I am thoroughly in sympathy with the Bill.
I think it is the most progressive piece of legislation which has been, introduced into this House since I entered it, barring perhaps the Railway Commission, and I do not know but it is broader than that. I have always been in favour of the Railway Commission, and in my constituency I have given the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition the greatest credit for establishing that commission, and have always recognized the good work it has done; and I believe that is an example of the good this Tariff Commission will do. I think that on both sides of the House we are reading into this Bill far more than it contains, because broad and big men aTe . not all in the manufacturing institutions, the railway institutions or any other particular institution. A broad and big man means a man familiar with the great work in which he is engaged, whatever it may be; and the personnel of this commission should be composed of men from at least two of the great classes in this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think there has been on the other side of the House a great deal of misapprehension as to what these

words, ' under the direction of the minister ' are intended to convey. In subsection 1 of section 4, the character of the information to be obtained by this commission is set forth in considerable detail. Then, subsection 2, in order to make the scope of the commission thoroughly comprehensive, declares that ' the commission shall make inquiry into any otner matter upon which the minister desires information, in relation to any goods wnich, if brought into Canada or produced in Canada, are subject to or exempt from duties of customs, and shall report to the minister.' The third subsection deals with inquiries under the Customs /vet. The fourth subsection enables, not the minister but the Governor in Council, to direct the commission to make inquiry into any other matter or thing in relation to the trade or commerce of Canada. No one can deny that the scope of the commission is pretty comprehensive. In the first subsection the character of the information which the commission is to obtain is stated in considerable detail. The subjects in respect of which the commission is to obtain that information are not enumerated. Take, for example, the item of agricultural implements, which has entered into every tariff which we have had in this country for many years. In some section of the country an agitation might arise with respect to the duties on agricultural implements. The commission might be going on in the ordinary course, without any particular direction from the minister, to make inquiry into this or that or the other item of the tariff. It would be competent for the Minister of Finance, by virtue of those words 1 under the direction of the minister,' to say to them: Drop everything else, and Investigate the conditions with regard to the production of agricultural implements In Canada, and ascertain whether or not, having regard, to the conditions of production in this country as compared with the conditions in other countries, the tariff is too high. It is precisely for the very reason to which my hon. friend calls attention that these words * under the direction of the minister ' have been inserted in the Bill. The ministers of the Crown are responsible to parliament, and responsible through parliament to the people of this country; and if the people of any particular district in the country should find themselves pressed by conditions which prevail under the tariff as it may exist at any time, it should be open to them to make representations to the Minister of Finance, and it would be proper for him, having regard to those representations, to direct an inquiry into that particular grievance to the exclusion of everything else for the time being. That is the object of the Bill; and, as I apprehend the mat-Mr. BORDEN.
ter, the omission of those words from the Bill would prevent the Minister of Finance from directing the attention and energies of the commission to the matter to which I have alluded or to similar matters that might at once demand the attention of the government and the inquiry of the Tariff Commission. That is the whole theory, as 1 understand it. The people will have a commission which can make these inquiries, it will be the right of the people at all times to make representations to the government through the minister in charge; and it will he the duty of the minister in charge, upon these representations, to direct a proper inquiry to be made by this commission into all the conditions both in this country and in other countries which ought to control the framing of a tariff in that regard.
Will the right hon. gentleman confirm what the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated, that the reports made by the commission would be laid before parliament on request?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is entirely my apprehension of the matter.

I think my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) is well advised in looking upon this Bill with some measure of suspicion. There has been so much protest as to what the Bill did not contain as to lead those of us who are, like my hon. friend from Souris, inclined to be suspicious, to think that perhaps after all there is something in it that is not disclosed on the surface; because often a Bill is important from what it does not contain rather than from what it does contain. I agree with my hon friend from Souris that the purpose in the mind of anyone who spoke in this country on behalf of a Tariff Commission was that it would give all classes of people in the country a fair deal. The hon. gentleman was particular to inquire as to where the farmers of the west came in, under the terms of this Bill. The right hon. the Prime Minister undertook to show him, but he did not find it and does not find it in the four corners of the Bill.
He said he did.
My hon. friend has just given this House an example of what this Bill is intended to do; as I said on the second reading, its purpose is to humbug the people of this country.
I do not think so for a moment.

My hon. friend is at liberty to have his own opinion, but I think the very statements he made to-day as to his understanding of the Bill and
[DOT]2973

as to what he understood the Prime Minister to say, is the evidence of that.

That is your opinion.
Mr. OLIVER, Because there is not within the four corners of the Bill anything to show that there is any provision or that provision will be made or can be made under that Bill for considering the interests of the farmers in the matter of the tariff. In section 4.

It is a question as between my hon. friend and myself as to the knowledge of the English language, and I declare that in section 4 there is nothing which contemplates the consideration of the interest of the farmer by the Tariff Commission.

Then there is no part of the section that contemplates going into the consideration of the condition of any class, it contemplates a consideration of the condition of the farmer as well as of any other class.
Mr. OLIVER, That is where my hon. friend is entirely mistaken and it is another evidence of the success of the Bill and its promoter in humbugging the people of the country. I think I can.

speechtext:

Read the definition at the beginning of the Act. Goods are treated of throughout the whole Act, and what do goods include? It is the farmer who is interested in tariff revision downward, and it is the man who represents the farmers and speaks for them, who is taking serious responsibility in supporting and advocating a measure which has no other purpose than to lay the foundation for a tariff revision upward, to lay more heavily than they lie to-day, the burdens of the tariff upon the farmer.
I am sorry my hon. friend from South York is not in the House. I wanted to agree with him as well as with the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner). We on this side are exactly at one with my hon. friend in this desire. That is our idea of the proper way of collecting information upon which the minister is to base liis revision of the tariff-to collect that information on his own responsibility and that of the government, and place it before parliament when called upon as a report of the department and the government, for which he and his officials are responsible. Each individual member must declare himself on that measure upon his responsibility Mr. OLIVER.
to his constituents. Therefore, every member of parliament is just as much entitled to the full information collected by a commission as the government is. And it' is because thisi means which is being taken by the government to collect information, is being taken in the name of parliament and under the name of a commission, when it is really, to all intents and purposes, departmental information, that we object to it. We say that if it is to be departmental, let it be departmental; and if it is to he a commission, let it be a commission.
