But, if our friends opposite do not wish 10 give us a commission of that kind, then let them get their information as a department on their responsibility which it is within their right to do and which is just as proper a method of collecting information a3 the other;-under the responsible system of government it is a more correct method. speechtext: House in Committee on Bill (No. 16), respecting patents of Thomas Wadge- Mr. Aikins.

It is quite apparent that the ordinary member, having this Bill placed before him after it has passed the Private Bills Committee, is hardly in a position to decide on its merits. Therefor, I think whoever is in charge of the Bill should make a full statement of the reasons for it.

I am not in charge of the Bill, but, in the absence of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins), I desire to state to the House what I understand to be the reasons for the Bill. It appears that Thomas Wadge purchased patent No. 73,790, being an improvement in grain separators, commonly called fanning mills. When Mr. Wadge purchased the patent through his solicitors in Winnipeg, Messrs. Metcalfe, Sharpe & Stackpoole, he had an investigation of the title made. Mr. Wadge understood, when he purchased the patent, that it had been taken out for the usual period of 18 years. This I understand was the statement of his solicitors. It was not until very recently, when he took possession of the actual letters patent, that he ascertained that an error had been made in the office of his solicitors, and that the fees had been paid for only 6 years. Under the patent law a patentee may pay the fees for a 6 years term, and, on the expiration of that term, may pay the balance of the fees for the whole life of the patent, which in Canada is 18 years. Consequently Mr. Wadge is under the necessity of applying to parliament for the continuance of the patent for the full term of 18 years. I have the affidavit of Mr. Wadge to the effect of the statement I have made to the House. I think I need not read this to the committee. It has been read in the Private Bills Committee, and they accepted it. I simply make this statement, from which it appears to me that Mr. Wadge is entitled to the relief asked for.
When did this patent first issue?
I cannot give the date of issue. There are two patents-No. 73,789 and No. 73,790. It was on the 29th of

March, 1904, that Mr. Wadge purchased them from the Twin City Separator Company, and he at once proceeded t'o manufacture, and has been manufacturing on a large scale since, and it was not until July, 1911, that he ascertained that his patents had lapsed by Teason of the error I have stated. So that it would appear that the patents were taken out only shortly before 1904.	*
Where does Mr. Wadge live?
The city of Winnipeg is the place of manufacture.

Has this Bill been examined by the Department of Agriculture? It has been customary in the past to have a report from that department in respect to Bills of this class, and that report has always had great weight with the committee. In connection with every Bill, so far as my observation has gone, the attitude of the committee has been: we should not do this, and it ends by saying, we will do it this time, but we will not do it again. But we have always required from the Minister of Agriculture some statement to the effect that the Bill is satisfactory to his department, which usually inquires to see whether there is some interest that may be affected, or whether there are patents of a like character that may become in some way prejudiced by the proposed renewal. While we certainly want to do justice to the one, we do not want to do injustice to the other. It seems to me we should have some representation from that department.

As a member of the Private Bills Committee, I remember the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, Mr. O'Halloran, being present, and being asked his opinion with reference to this and other Bills of a similar nature. His reply was that the policy of the department was adverse to the passing of private legislation of this character, but that the Private Bills Committee', and the House invariably overrides the policy of the department in that respect, where the, negligence is that, not of the individual, but of the solicitor.

Suppose we tried the experiment of refusing to pass this Bill and forced Mr. Wadge to go back to his solicitors, would it have a good and salutary effect? Would that not have the salutary effect of reducing the number of these Bills coming, before parliament, would it not remind solicitors that they might be called upon to respond if they did not give attention to such matters?

I understood the deputy Minister of Agriculture to say that once
[DOT]2935

you admit the principle of renewing expired patents there was no reason why this one should not be renewed. From the evidence there is no doubt that this is a going concern manufacturing large quantities and the proprietors would be damaged to some extent if this was not renewed.

We should have from the Department of Agriculture a statement on their responsibility that this is a going concern and that "there is no conflict of right between this establishment and some other of which we have no knowledge. I would be strongly in favour of passing the Bill on the merits as stated, but I think we should have some such assurance from the department.

It has not been the habit of any department in relation to the Bills within its purview to go into the questions of fact and make itself responsible for such statements as that the concern is a going concern. That fact appeared to be established by evidence before the committee. The solicitors in charge of the matter are a very responsible, good and careful firm in Winnipeg. The head of the firm was recently appointed a judge of the Court of King's Bench by the late government. I would not like to have it go out from anything I have said that they were guilty^ in this case beyond what is inevitable in a large office occasionally. I think it would be a hardship to Mr. Wadge if the relief were not granted. As to the conflict of rights no one else could manufacture lawfully until the expiry of the patent and any one who has commenced the manufacture since its expiry is protected under section 2 of the Act.

speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 84) respecting certain patents of ' Thomas D. Rambaut.- Mr. Ames.
I would again suggest that the member having charge of the Bill should make an explanation for the convenience of the committee.

This Bill which was very carefully considered in the Private Bills Committee is one for keeping alive a patent now possessed by Thomas D. Rambaut. The circumstances in this case are very exceptional. The original patent was granted to William Ernest Cook, who in due course undertook to transfer the patent as he had a right to do, to Thomas D. Rambaut. Rambaut on legal advice concluded that his title-was not altogether good. He went back to Cook to get his title made good, but found Cook seriously ill, in fact on his death bed, unable to sign his name, or in
any way deal further with it. Cook died shortly afterwards and there then followed considerable litigation as to who were the heirs, and during this time Rambaut, not being certain that the patent was his, did not want to spend money on it. By the time he found that his title to the patent was valid, the period in which manufacture must be commenced in Canada had expired. He, therefore, made petition to the committee, the committee heard the claim and unanimously decided that the case was so exceptional that a further opportunity should be given to him to manufacture. No one has done any manufacturing or used the patents in Canada so it does not in any way infringe on any rights.
What is the device?

A patent process for dessi-cating vegetables, and we have documentary evidence that if this patent is kept alive an important company is prepared to come into Canada, build a factory, and at once give employment in the manufacture of dried vegetables in the method herein described. We felt it would be an advantage to have the industry giving employment to workmen and giving an opportunity to farmers to sell their vegetables. No objections were taken to the Bill, even the departmental officers said that while they took generally an attitude of uncordiality towards requests of this kind there were no special reasons why in such a case as this the application should not be granted.
I see that Rambaut is a citizen of New York. Is there any suspicion underlying this that would in any way affect our constitution?
I do not think there is any fear of the subversion of the constitution in this particular case.
What was the result of the litigation, was it decided that Rambaut had the legal title to the patent, or would we be legislating away the rights that might belong to Cook's heirs?

It was subsequently found that the transfer was legal, and it was with the full consent of Cook's heirs that Rambaut undertook to commence the manufacture. Then, after his death, when the estate was settled up, it was, with the full consent of the heirs that Mr. Rambaut proceeded to utilise the patent which came to him by regular transfer. -
When did the patent expire?
My recollection is that it expired on the 16th February. 1911.
That is the expiration of the period for commencing manufacture?
It was registered in the Patent Office, 16th September, 1911.
Is this legislation being secured with the knowledge and consent of the heirs of Mr. Cooke, the original patentee?
Such were the representations made to us in the committee by the promoters of the Bill.
What was the character of the evidence submitted?
I think the solicitor for Mr. Rambaut had with him documents to that effect. I know he said he was prepared to submit evidence for every allegation he made in connection with the Bill.

I must say as one member of this committee, I am not altogether satisfied with the explanation. This is a matter which is so perfectly plain. Mr. Rambaut controlled this patent from Mr. Cooke, and had the documents whatever they might be. There is no reason why Mr. Rambaut should not have begun manufacturing in Canada within the two years allowed, or have obtained the necessary extension of time which the department has the right to give under certain conditions. He did not do it. He remained asleep on his rights. This is not at all in the same category with the case of Thomas Wadge. In that case, we have a citizen of Canada, carrying on a legitimate business, who finds that, through the fault of his solicitor his patent has expired. But here we have a bunch of New York fellows. We don't know whether they are genuine or not. They have not spent a dollar in Canada, and probably will not. But they want to sell out and make some money. Why, if I had half the nerve that my hon. friend has shown, within the last year I could have made a lot of money. A man from the state of Maine came to me and wanted to get legislation to renew a patent which had expired under circumstances not nearly so barefaced as this. But I was so modest that I told him I could not ask parliament to renew his rights when those rights had been lost through his own carelessness. I do not think that the parliament of Canada has a right to grant such concessions to these people. Why, Mr. Chairman, you know we do not love Americans nowadays-
Under which flag?
I think there is strong reason for opposing the passing of this Bill.

As I read this Bill, it does not affect the rates as be-Mr. AMES.
tween Cooke's heirs and Rambaut; it leaves the legal status of the parties where _ it was, simply revives the patent rates involved. The Deputy Minister of Agriculture was present in the committee and gave the same opinion with respect to this Bill as with respect to the previous one. Rambaut acted upon the advice of his solicitor which was that this assignment was valid. It is true that, under these circumstances, he slept on his rights. But when the matter was investigated, he found that he was out of court unless fie could get this special legislation. ' It seems to me that this is on all fours with the previous Bill.

I think that this is not on all fours with the previous Bill. In that ease manufacturers had already taken action to a very large extent, with a large capital outlay, and every evidence of bona fides. In this case, it looks a little like a speculation in patent rights, a kind of speculation more common in the United States than in Canada. It would appear to me that Rambaut had made a speculative purchase of certain rights, and, after the deal had gone through simply slept on his rights, not thinking it worth while to comply with the Canadian law, even to the extent of getting the necessary extension of time. I suppose that now he sees the chance to transfer his patent to some one else and make something out of it. He has spent no money in Canada, has done nothing to make good on this patent; and I for one take the ground that patents are not to be lightly renewed under these circumstances.

Let us see what will be the logical outcome if the advice of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) were followed. Hei'e is a concern that is prepared to come to Canada and make an investment for the manufacture of an important article, establishing an industry that will employ Canadian Labour and give a market for Canadian producers of agricultural products. Through no fault of his own, but through an error of his legal adviser, he finds he is debarred from using the patent which he has had assigned to him for valid considerations. Are we going to say that on that technicality we will deprive him of the opportunity of coming to Canada and manufacturing as I have suggested? Is it wise to do so? On the otlier hand, what interest is going to be injured by passing this Bill? No one has attempted to use this patent in the country. Either this man will use it or it will not be used. And by granting this legislation no one else's rights are infringed upon in the slightest degree.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames) say that he personally knows that these people are coming here to manufacture?
There was filed with the commission by a thoroughly responsible party, a written statement to that effect, and that satisfied the committee unanimously, so far as I could see.
But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames) does not know personally?
I know Thomas D. Rambaut personally, and I know him to be a thoroughly responsible party.

My hon. friend (Mr. Ames) would make this committee believe that if this man's patent is not revived, he cannot enter into the manufacture of this article. Why, it is the very reverse. Not only can Rambaut manufacture the article, | but any man in Canada can manufacture it. I would point out to my hon. friend that a man has the right to manufacture an article exclusively, under patent only when the law gives him that right. In the absence of the patent, everybody has the right to manufacture it. This is an improvement that is well known to the public. I presume it is patented in the United States; it has been patented in Canada for five years. So, the public know about it. How do we know how many men are standing up with capital ready to enter upon this manufacture and build up a business in Canada? I think the hon. gentleman is trying to prevent the carrying on of industries in Canada, rather than encouraging them. The strongest reason I have heard for opposing the Bill is the reason my hon. friend has given why we should pass it.

I would suggest that we act in this matter as the Railway Commission frequently acts; -where there is a pledge as to what they are going to do we require them to put up a deposit. We will take ' greenbacks ' in this instance, we won't require a gold deposit..

I can't see what good object can be served in treating this Bill in a different wiay from what you are treating other Bills of the same character. This person has acted in perfect good faith from the outset. It was erroneous advice given him by his advocate, which he afterwards discovered to be inaccurate, that ted to his losing his rights in the matter. He was under the impression that his patent was not laltogether valid, and that it was necessary for him to secure additional signatures on the part of the original owner of the patent, Mr. William Cook. Immediately he discovered this fact he sought Mr. Cook, but Mr. Cook was in extremis and was unable to sign the papers necessary therewith. If Mr. Oook had been alive and well and the additional papers had been signed, the result would have been that *everything would have been complied with
by Mr. Rambaut, and there would have been no necessity for this Bill. But that is the way the case stands to-day. It seems to me tliat we would be creating a precedent in this Bill quite different from that we have followed in other cases, if we said that this Bill should not go through. I may say that the departmental officials that were present with us from the Department of Agriculture raised no serious objection to this Bill, any more than they would raise to any other Bill of a similar character. I have seen much more strenuous opposition to. other Bills than was taken in this particular case. I do not see why the opposition should deem it advisable to single out this particular Bill for slaughter.
I think we had better let. it go through.

I take exception to the statement that this Bill is on all fouTS with the Bill we agreed to a few minutes ago. The conditions are absolutely different, and the reasons that made it proper to pass the other Bill are reasons which make it improper to pass this Bill. I;f this committee has any responsibility at all it should not permit legislation of this character to go through, unless there are better reasons given for it than we have heard As has been suggested by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), however good the intent of the applicant may be, on the face of the Bill it would appear to be purely a speculative investment, that f.e has not shown good faith, and is not entitled to consideration. The refusal of the committee to pass the Bill will not in any way injure the industries or the welfare of Canada, 'although it may do some injury to this man, who is responsible for his own undoing if he does not get what he wants.

In the previous case, the man had made an investment, he was manufacturing, and if you did not give him legislation, he would have been seriously interfered with, and perhaps his investment would have been depreciated in value. _ In this case, you do not affect any such right, but by refusing to this man the privileges which he seeks, you do not give him an advantage over others, who apparently, have just as much right to the privilege of manufacturing this {particular commodity for preserving vegetables, as would the gentleman named in the Bill, Mr. Rambaut. This becomes a serious matter when you consider that you may be depriving Canadian citizens of a privilege which certainly will be theirs if this legislation does not go through.

I do not want to block the committee in coming to a conclusion, but I think if ever, in my experience in this House, a case has been presented for the renewal of a patent which absolutely lacks

merit., it is this case. It is true that in the past we have been rather lenient in granting applications for renewal, where rights have lapsed. But in all the cases I can recall, there has been some merit to the application, there has been some investment of money, something has been done by the owner or the promoter. But here is a case, where peciple deliberately slept on their rights for four or five years, did not take enough interest in the matter to see whether they were the owners or not, until the time has lapsed during which they are entitled to manufacture goods in this country under a patent. It we grant this renewal, we grant to a body of United States patent speculators and promoters the right to come into Canada and manufacture on the basis of a monopoly, under a patent right, at all events. They have not made out any case strong enough to justify such action in this parliament, and I do not believe that hon. members opposite think they have either. Had they gone ahead with an investment, had they placed their money here within the last two or three years, as they might have done, and shown some bona fides in the matter, the case would have been entirely different. But if you grant this patent right to those New Yorkers, it excludes Canadians from entering into that line of manufacture in Canada, and I am opiposed to it on that particular ground. If other patents come up with no more merit than the present one, I will have no hesitation in opposing them also.

On more careful reading of the Bill, I want to give another reason why I oppose it. It seems to me that it is the most vicious renewal of a patent right I have ever seen since I have been in parliament. This man some years ago bought a patent. He says, according to the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), he was afraid that his rights might not be perfect, and he tried to get a new document from Mr. Cook.
He had rights in that, however, under which he could justify the manufacture of these goods in Canada. He did not do so. He went on for five years. Now, they come in with this Bill and they propose not only placing this man in the same position as he was in when he got the right from Mr. Cooke, but they give him two years in order to exercise the right of manufacture, and they do more than that because I am satisfied that, under clause 2 of this Bill, they are giving him rights which are not in his patent at all. They are bringing him under the provisions of that section of the Patent Act which gives tue commissioner the right to excuse him from manufacturing the article so long as he holds himself in readiness to grant the license to some other man to manufacture it and Mr. GUTHRIE.
pay him a royalty. The more you examine this clause the more you see that it is something which ought not to be granted to a Canadian citizen, let alone to a foreigner. Yon are placing this man in the same position as if he had come to Canada to-day for the first time, was the original inventor of this process and applied to the _ Patent Office in the ordinary course of business to get his patent. If he had done that they could not have given him one day longer, they could not have given mm one more advantage than they are giving him under this Bill. They are allowing this man to have slept upon his rights for five years, they are preventing the people from enjoying this invention, they are preventing people from entering into the manufacture of this article, they are placing this man in the same position as he would have been if he had been the inventor of this article and they are giving him rights and privileges which the original patent did not give at all. But, they give him something that is provided in the amendment which was made to the Patent Act in 1997. I think that if there ever was a ease in which an American citizen has come over here and presumed upon our innocence it is the case of this man coming here and wanting this patent renewed.

Now I will state my objection as briefly as possible. I would like the promoter of the Bill to give me some information as to whether the original patent is entitled to the provisions of the latter part of clause 2. Section. 44 of the Patent Act is as follows:
On the application of the applicant for a patent, previous to the issue thereof, or on the application within six months after the issue of a patent of the patentee or his legal representatives, the commissioner, having Tegard to the nature of the invention, may order that snch patent, instead of being subject to the condition with respect to the construction and manufacture of the patented invention hereinbefore provided, shall be subject to the following conditions.
Without taking time to read these conditions I may explain that they mean that the commissioner can absolve the manufacturer or the patentee from the necessity of manufacturing, so long as he will agree to grant a license to other people to manufacture. I would like to know if the original patent comes under that provision of section 44 of the Patent Act, chapter 69 of the Revised Statutes.
I cannot tell the hon. gentleman that. I can only say that this is the standard clause which you will find in a great many other Bills of a similar character.
That was not in the Thomas Wedge patent which we just revived a few moments ago.
It was not necessary in that case.

It was not in it. and .it seems we are giving this man rights 95
which he is not entitled to. We are giving him a better patent than his patent really calls for. Surely, if we place him where he was before Bis negligence, he has no right to come to this country and ask for more; he has no right to ask us to put him in a position in which he may never manufacture this article in Canada or in which we may never have that industry so long as he holds himself ready to permit the manufacture and reap the benefit of the royalty from it?

It is a matter of serious moment as to whether or not we should place this man in a better position than he was entitled to at the incaption of his patent.

House resumed in committee on Bill (No. 88) to provide for the appointment of a Tariff Commission.-Mr. White (Leeds).
On section 4.

When the House rose at six o'clock, I was discussing section 4, and pointing out that there were matters of serious importance in connection with the tariff that, in my judgment, were not contemplated to be dealt with by the commission appointed under this Bill. It was stated by the Minister of Finance that these matters did, as a matter of fact, come under the provisions of this section, but even admitting that statement to be correct, I still hold that so far as the reading of the section on its face is concerned, and so far as the discussion upon the Bill has gone, there is no indication whatever that this Bill was intended in any degree, to cover that side of tariff legislation, present or prospective, to which I was drawing attention. I was drawing attention to the loss that has been suffered by the producers of the west in the defeat of the reciprocity arrangement, under which they would have secured free access to the United States market. I gave a statement of the difference in price on barley and wheat as between Fort William and Minneapolis, and in the case of wheat I gave the price of nine cars actually bought on the Minneapolis sample' market, and the samples examined in Winnipeg by competent men and the grades and prices attached and it would appear that the spread or loss to the Canadian farmer between Fort William and Minneapolis ran from eight cents to thirty-seven cents per bushel. Assuming that the average loss is fifteen cents per bushel, and assuming on the statement of Mr. Thompson of the Ogilvie Milling Company that there are some fifty million bushels of grain in the west still to market, the western Canadian



farmer stands to lose by failure to secure free access to the United States market for his wheat, seven and a half million dollars.
When?

Since the 21st of September. This, it seems to me is a matter of sufficient importance to warrant the attention of the government and of the Minister of Finance. A dead loss of seven and a half million dollars, not in watered stock, but in actual cash value, cannot be contemplated without serious thought by any one who has regard for the wellbeing of this country. This loss of seven ' and a half million dollars on one-third of the farmer's crop which he has for sale in this bad year is equal to the prospective profit on the one hundred million dollars of common stock representing no value which has been loaded upon the industrial activities of -Canada by the merger interests within the past three years. The farmer is actually losing in this one year, on one-third of his wheat crop as much money as these people hoped in their wildest dreams to make on these stupendous speculative organizations that they have been going into for the past three years. I have said and I verily believe that the purpose of the government, the purpose of the Minister of Finance, and the purpose of the Bill, is to find some way whereby interest can be earned on that one hundred millions of watered stock of absolutely no value. The Minister of Finance is bending all his attention to that end; he is going to appoint a commission that will cost this country in salaries alone $24,500; which will cost no doubt an equal amount in ordinary expenses for the members of the commission, and there will have to be a staff added at what expense we do not know. In the case of the United States body, which he takes for his example, the latest report that we have is that their staff numbers over seventy, and if the Minister of Finance continues to follow along the lines of that organization, this country will be lucky if it gets out of this precious Tariff Commission with an expenditure of less than one hundred thousand dollars a year; and all with the ultimate purpose of giving value where no value was, and of laying that much of extra tax upon the shoulders of the people of this country. Now, he does not need any Tariff Commission, and he does not need any one hundred thousand a year expenditure; he does not need any expert evidence to find a means to save to the farmers of the west the seven and a half million dollars to which I have called attention.
There is to-day on the statute-books of the United States a law which says that if -and when the Canadian government iM. OLIVER.
makes provisions which are parallel to those of that law, it shall come into effect, and the effect of the law would be to put $7,500,000, at a minimum calculation, into the pockets of the producers of the western prairies, and through their pockets into the currents and channels of trade and industry and commerce and transportation all through the Dominion of Canada. May I believe that the suggestion is at any rate worthy of some consideration, which, so far as the form of the Bill or any indication of intent on the part of the government is concerned, has not entered into their calculations at all. But wheat is not the only grain affected. I might mention a little item which I gathered from the ' Pioneer Express ' of Pembina, North Dakota. which makes this statement-
From November 1 to December 20 there have been imported into this district from Canada 138,062 bushels of barley, which paid duty at the rate of 30 cents a bushel, which duty amounted to $41,418. The most of this barley is marketed direct by Canadian farmers who are contiguous to the line.
The barley crop of the western prairie provinces is estimated by Sir Byron E. Walker at 37,000,000 bushels this year. It is not to be supposed that the whole of that crop is for sale. A large part of it is grown for feed purposes, but it is a well-known fact that this year a considerable amount of the wheat of the western prairies is only fit for feed, while the barley is of good quality, and it would be a happy condition if we were able to-send our barley to the United States markets free of the 30 cent duty and use our feed wheat for the purposes for which barley weuld otherwise be used. I am informed that last year the United States used 150,000,000 bushels of barley, and there is every reason to believe that its market would absorb every bushel of barley the Canadian west could spare, and at prices which would not only give our people the United States only, but a handsome profit over and above the duty.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. We are discussing clause 4, and the rule says that speeches in Committee of the Whole must-be strictly relevant to the clause under discussion. I submit that the hon. gentleman has for the last ten minutes been out of order.

We have been discussing the question of the responsibility of the government in regard to the commission, and I have been pointing out that the government, in the discharge of its responsibility, is not taking consideration of one of the most important features of the tariff. I think I am quite within the limits of the section, but I have not com-

pleted ray argument, and if my hen. friend will only have patience, I think I will demonstrate to him and the whole committee that every word I have said is absolutely pertinent to section 4.
I would ask the ruling of the Chair.

I certainly will bow to the ruling of the Chairman if he says that I am not entitled to use the arguments I am making, but I certainly am well wdthin the example of other members who have spoken on different sections of the Bill, and I W'ould respectfully ask that I be not restricted more than other members. As I have the honour to. represent one of the most strictly agricultural counties in the Dominion of Canada, I may be permitted to say a word in regard to this Bill. The Bill presented to this House by the hon. Minister of Finance is one of the most important as well as one of the most logical pieces of legislation which has ever been presented to the parliament of Canada. I believe that the carrying out of this idea of the appointment of a Tariff Commission as outlined in this Bill will result in great good to the agriculturists of Canada.
Hon. gentlemen opposite throughout this debate have 'endeavoured to make it appear that this Bill was designed entirely for the benefit of the manufacturers, that they were the only class who could be referred to by the Bill. The hon. gentlemen from Edmonton, Humboldt and Assiniboia, have all advanced this idea and they have aai object in view, that of trying to create the impression in this country that tire Conservative government is here in the interests of the manufacturers and is opposed to the farmers.

I rise to a point of order. I assume that you are 954
anxiously waiting for some gentleman to call attention to the fact that the hon. gentleman is not speaking to the clause before the committee.

speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to refer to the Bill. He is apparently discussing the principle of the Bill. I would remind the hon. gentleman that he must speak on clause 4.

I fully expected this little act of courtesy from jny hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). I should have referred to section 4, which is a very important section, it must be a very important section because it has been discussed at such great length by hon. gentlemen opposite. I have been surprised at the conclusions arrived at in the discussion of .section 4 of this very important measure. Some hon. gentlemen have drawn from section 4 of this Bill the conclusion that it was designed solely in the interests of the manufacturers. The hon. member for Humboldt made this assertion notwithstanding the statements previously made by the Minister of Finance. The minister said:
We do not desire to be relieved from responsibility with regard to the tariff, and all the Tariff Commission does, is to enable us to obtain information on which to act.
That was very explicit. He said further:
I think the report of the Tariff Commission should be available to every member of this House as well as to the ministers, and then no doubt it will carry great weight. But that is far from saying that it is absolutely conclusive.
The Finance Minister further said:
I would be the last man to suggest that the House of Commons should he denied the information obtained by means of the expenditure which they have authorized. There is no intention of that kind in this Bill. My hon. friends have been simply raising spectres with regard to this Bill.
Notwithstanding these very clear and specific assertions on the part of the minister, hon. gentlemen opposite have stated repeatedly just the opposite of what the minister has said. The hon. member for Edmonton could not see wherein this clause of the Bill had any reference to the farmer. One would infer from his remarks that farmers were not even thought of when the Bill was brought before the House, that there was no possibility of the farmer getting consideration of his wrongs. I do not think the hon. gentleman was justified in coming to that conclusion. Take the various sections of this clause, they clearly set out that in respect of goods produced in or imported into Canada, and you will note it does not say in respect of some goods,'but, in respect of goods, which has

the same meaning as if the word * all ' was prefixed to goods-in respect of goods produced in or imported into Canada the commission shall, under the direction of the minister, make inquiry, &c. The word * goods ' is very clearly defined in the beginning of the Bill and the definition makes it clear that this Bill is not confined to the consideration of manufactured articles. There is a great chance for the farmers to be benefited by the 'appointment of a Tariff Commission. Take, for instance, the question of wheat. There is a duty at present of 12 cents a bushel on wheat. ' The United States has a duty of 25 cents a *bushel on wheat- Is it mot right that information should he obtained as to the [DOT]cost of production, the cost of transportation, to the place of consumption; is it not right that the Canadian farmer should have, in fairness to himself, some protection against wheat produced, for instance, in Argentina?
Hear, hear.
Did I catch a whisper from the horn, member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that sounded like ' hear, hear ?'
Hear, hear.

And yet the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) strongly supported on the 21st of last September a proposal which would have denied to the farmers of Canada the very thing that he says ' hear, hear ' for now.
In order that the hon. gentleman may not be under any misapprehension, 1 meant the ' hear, hear ' sarcastically.

I suppose the hon. member wishes me to regard even a little sarcastic reference from himself in the way of a compliment.

Is it fair that the farmers of this country who have to pay the rate of wages they do should be asked to compete on even terms with the farmers of Argentina who pay wages at the rate of 64 cents a day?

Now that contention is not borne out by the history of the Conservative party, or by the history of the Liberal party. I could refer to many acts and expressions in the history of the Liberal party to show that that was not the case. The duty on agricultural implements, up to 1907, was 20 per cent, and it was left there by the Liberal party as they found it in 1896. In 1907 the Fielding tariff was brought down, that was the year before a general election, and they reduced the duty on agricultural implements from 20 to 174 per cent. But at the same time they raised the value for duty purposes of binders, for instance, whereby they collected a duty of 17J per cent which amounted to more than they previously collected with a duty of 20 per cent. At the same time they appealed to the farmers for support on the ground that they had begun to carry out the policy they had advocated for IS years previous to 1896, the policy of destroying (protection entirely. eminent, the right hon. leader of the opposition, in answering those gentlemen, said that there was one thing at least the Liberal party prided itself on, they were proud of the fact that they had been very careful not to do anything to disturb the manufacturers of this country. I have said something as to the magnitude of the case; may I say something now as to the urgency of the case. The Manitoba ' Free Press ' has been making an investigation of the conditions as to the marketable wheat in the prairie provinces, and I have before me the issue of February 10th instant, in which I find a despatch from Harris, Sask., a portion of which I shall read. I think when I have read it the House will agree that the matter is urgent and is worthy of the attention of the government in the most marked degree. The article reads as follows:
Harris, Sask., Feb. 7.-This afternoon at Harris I saw a sight that has surely seldom been witnessed on the western prairies. I saw 100,000 bushels of wheat piled in the railway yard like coal. It was in rough bin9 made of lumber. The bins have been built on the ground with no foundation but mother earth, and the only roof is a mantle of snow. Most of the bins contain from 500 to 1,000 bushels, but one of them, which looked from the outside something like a roofless rink or a large cattle pen inclosed 50,000 bushels of wheat. This wheat a local lumber company had had to accept from the farmers in lieu of cash. Besides the bins there were in the yards about a dozen grain wagons all full of wheat, and I am informed that every available nook and corner in Harris is stored with wheat.
A large quantity of lumber has been used in the construction of these emergency bins. None of them could have been, erected for less than $50, while the large one must have cost very much more. The idea, of erecting the bins is to have the wheat in hand the moment anything in the shape of a freight car presents itself at Harris. To-day the yard was as [DOT] bare of cars as Minitonas was of gold, and I understand that that has been the condition, of things for some days past. There were 141 cars on the order hook to-day, but that by no means represents the number wanted. Many farmers need three or four cars, hut cannot order more than one at a time. About 308 cars of grain, practically all wheat, have been shipped from here since the season opened. Last year only 192 cars were shipped from this point.
Since the middle of December all cars with the exception of four have been loaded from the temporary bins above described. Much of this wheat is tough. Worse still, there are at least 75,000 bushels of wheat lying on the farm in heaps, just as it came from the separator. Most of it is tough and will spoil if it. is not got out during the next few weeks. At present the cars are coming into Harris at the rate of four or five a week, a rate which is entirely inadequate, and which will mean heavy loss unless it is speedily increased. The three elevators have been full continuously. It is claimed by the railway company that only 7,000,000 were estimated for the Goose Lake line, whereas the actual crop has turned out to be nearer 14,000,000.
The business men of Harris are weary of waiting for cars which come not. In the meantime, there is financial constipation, or as one should say, ' nothing doing.' In all the stores and in the hotel notices are up, 'Positively no credit. We have closed our books.' If the grocery store adhered strictly to this rule, there would be actual starvation or suffering in the neighbourhood, hut it does not. In other stores the rule of ' No credit ' is closely followed. Clerks have little to do and pass the time chatting with farm hands who are waiting for the farmers to sell their grain and pay them their wages. I talked to-day to Thomas A. Stevenson, a Harris farmer, who told me that he finished threshing 2,000 bushels just before Christmas. His wheat had quite a bit of ice in it. After threshing it was placed in bins in the field. The wheat was still in the bins. He had put his name down for a car immediately after threshing, and there were still two pages of the order book ahead of him.
Now, I think I have established that the condition is one of stupendous magnitude, that it is a case of extreme urgency; and if our hon. friends say that the tariff has nothing to do with that condition, I can only reply that the tariff has everything t-o do with it-that had it not been for the tariff it would have been possible to have delivered every bushel of the wheat that is now left without shelter on those western prairies, safely at some terminal point, either Fort William, Duluth or Minneapolis, before the spring caime that

would destroy all the damp wheat that remained at that time.
Is not that wheat permitted to go into the United States in bond to be ground for export free of duty?

No. At the present time the duty is paid, and it is refunded after the wheat is ground; but up to the present time the railway rates, in addition to the duty, have been such as practically to prevent that being done on any large scale. If the railway rates were suitable, no doubt a great deal of the grain could be absorbed in that way. But that is a very inadequate remedy for the terrible condition that prevails to-day. What was needed was that every possible avenue should have been opened, not only the privilege of grinding in bond, but the privilege of grinding for home consumption, and, what is more urgent, the privilege of entry for feed purposes. But that has not been done, and the condition which I have described prevails all over the western country. And my hon. friend the Minister of Finance brings down a Bill which absolutely ignores on the face of it the interests that are represented in that condition of affairs. I cannot agree that such a provision is satisfactory or is in accordance with the wellbeing of the country.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that a part of that grain was cut but unthreshed?
Yes.

That could not have been got out until it was threshed; but will the hon. gentleman tell me what purpose a farmer would have in threshing grain that was standing in the stook when, after having threshed it, he would have to put it in "a bin where it would remain until it was heated and destroyed, because he could not transport it?
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him again-
Will the hon. gentleman answer my question?

It is the government which my hon. friend supports, which has been in power since the 21.st of September, and since this condition began to exist, and I have placed before the government to-night a course which they could and Mr. OLIVER.
should have taken in order to have remedied that condition.
But even yet if they would take that course it could well be remedied in some measure. However, I have no hope from anything I see in this Bill or from anything I have heard here spoken from the other side of the House that any such action will be taken. While the wheat, which is practically the gold of our country, upon which not only the western farmer but the trade and commerce and industry and finance of this whole country depend, is depreciating in value, and may, in large measure, be actually lost, this government (brings in a Tariff Commission Bill upon which they propose to found a tariff at some time in the distant future, and that is their answer to this condition that exists. My hon. friend thought that opposition to this Bill was something of a pillow fight, that there was not any sincerity in it. May I return the compliment to him, and may I say that the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. White), who sits comfortably here in Ottawa, who spends more or less of his time in adjusting offices in the various departments of the public service while the country is in the condition that I have described, and it is in the power of the government to remedy that condition, stands in much the same position as Nero fiddling while Rome burned.
I do not want any member of this House to think that the conditions are exaggerated by me. I want the House to understand that these conditions are so serious that neither newspaper nor public man has dared to give full effect to the facts in regard to these conditions up to the present time, and I am at a loss to understand a government which sits quiet and still, knowing, absolutely knowing, that these conditions do exist.

much more drastic piece of legislation would have been presented, one which would have deprived this House *of a great many more of its functions than does the present measure. I stated that the address of the Minister of Trade and Commerce was illuminative. It was. And I think it was instructive to his own colleagues. Fortunately or unfortunately the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster, North Toronto), had not heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. White, Leeds), speak or the right hon. the leader of the government (Mr. Borden), this afternoon; and when asked by myself his interpretation of section 4 of this Bill, he gave an answer which coincided exactly with what I had said this afternoon, which had been challenged or contradicted by the hon. the Minister of Finance and by the right hon. the leader of the government.
That was in regard to the question as to whether this commission, when reporting was to report to the minister or to parliament. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said distinctly it was to report to parliament, for the use of members of parliament. That is the suggestion which I asked the Finance Minister and the Prime Minister to accept. When challenged on it, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, certainly, that was his understanding of it when he discussed it with his colleagues. Passing from that point, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said to the House: Let us go to the genesis of this movement in favour of the appointment of a Tariff Commission, let us see wiiere this demand comes from. Now I ask any hon. member of this House to state where the demand does come from. Is there a demand at all, apart from one source? The Minister of Trade and Commerce premised his remarks by saying that there was a demand, and I will ask the Prime Minister now, where is the demand from? I ask the Minister of Finance, where does , the demand come from? The only answer they give is the resolutions and various discussions of the Manufacturers' Association. My right hon. friend says that he has spoken some forty times throughout Canada, and has mentioned it in his speeches. But I submit there is no demand, and there has been no demand; and I ask hon. gentlemen opposite to give us a chance and adjourn this debate for even two or three weeks, to allow the country to become familiar with the terms of the Bill, because I take it that ninety per cent of the electors know nothing at all about it, and ninety iper cent of the newspapers of Canada have never discussed it. If we could only have a respite of two or three weeks, the government would know what kind of a demand there was for or against it.
Now how does the Minister of Trade and Commerce justify clause 4? He says that

in his time, back before the year 1896, he and a number of his colleagues were sent from province to province to gather information, to hear deputations, to hear ex parte statements through deputations, accompanied by lawyers, by huge piles of documents and reports of evidence. He says that when he.concluded his peregrinations he knew less about the tariff than he did when he started, and was less able to produce a perfect document than when he commenced his investigation. Then he says he came down to the House with a tariff made by rule of thumb. That was the predicament he was in. He has never made the confession before, but he has been challenged to do so. Hitherto he has always _ justified that tariff, and told us how, with one stroke of the pen, he wiped out four .millions of taxation. Now he says that after three or four months travel throughout the country he came down with a tariff made practically by guesswork. Is it any wonder that conditions detrimental (fco Canada followed such a tariff as that, that the revenue went down and the expenditure went up, that there was business stagnation throughout the country under a tariff made in the manner described by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, made, as he says, by rule of thumb. Then he had the audacity to say that if Mr. Fielding was in the House he would admit that his tariffs were similarly made. I challenge that statement. If Mr. Fielding were in the House to-day there would be no stronger opponent of this measure. Mr. Fielding's tariff was not made by any rule of thumb, it was made after careful and critical investigation. It was made, it is true, after a prolonged course of travel throughout the country, after much thought and _ consideration. It was made after obtaining the facts and information which any Minister of Finance should obtain. His tariff stood practically from 1907, until the present moment, and take it year by year from the date upon which it was passed, and all classes of this country I believe will accord it united praise. It left Canada on the 21st of September last in such a good condition that the Prime Minister was one of the champions of that stock in trade remark during the last election, ' let well enough alone.'
Now the Minister of Trade and Commerce did disagree with me in regard to striking out the words ' under the direction of the minister.' I still hold to my opinion that these words should be stricken out; I still hold that the Tariff Board should be an independent board. If the Finance Minister will put in an alternative clause there, I will be perfectly satisfied, though still protesting against the general principle. If he will allow an alternative clause enabling, say, five or ten individuals to request the Tariff Board to make an investigation into this, or that subject, I will be satisfied. But if he leaves it in its present form it is most highly objectionable, because any board he may see fit to appoint will be his own creation, subject only to his own direction, men who cannot in tire very nature of things make what may be called an independent finding. Now, if the Minister of Finance is sincere, he will admit some alternative clause, or will consent to strike out these words, and rely upon clause 2, which gives him every power imaginable over the board. Then leave the commissioners free under subsection 1, or put in an alternative clause allowing five or ten individuals, whoi make a bona fide application, to have this, that, or the other investigation held by this Tariff Commission. I have tak'en advice of the Speaker with regard to this, and I understand I can move several amendments. My first amendment then will be to strike out the words I have mentioned in subsection 1; ' under the direction of the minister.' Then coming down to clause (g) of subsection 1, my amendment will be to strike out the two last words ' the minister,' and insert the word ' parliament.' At present it reads ' report to the minister,' and I think the wisdom of the House will be with me in my suggestion that the report ought to be made to parliament. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that was his idea from the discussion he had with his colleagues in council.
How would my hon. friend reconcile subsection 6 with section 5, where it speaks of confidential evidence that must not be made public?
We will have a good deal to say on that section.
Does the hon. gentleman expect confidential evidence to be submitted to the House?

I have a good deal to say on confidential evidence. I do not believe in confidential evidence in a matter of this kind. I believe the facts on which the government is going to act should be made public to everybody. But I do think, in all fairness to the individual members of this House, outside of government circles, that the report should come down to parliament to enable us to judge, and not be in the nature of secret departmental information to be given solely to the Minister of Finance.
The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) proved my case. He said that this was the forum for disputants to come to, both parties could meet, thresh

the matter out, all parties would know what the facts were and the facts would be public and come down to this House so that we could all examine them. Why not abide by that? The request is reasonable and if the request is not granted it makes me feel that there is an ulterior motive in the mind of the Minister of Finance in regard to this Bill and that our criticism that there is something behind the Bill is only too well founded.
Then, I come to the next amendment that I am going to move and that is to strike out subsection 3 altogether. Subsection 3 is the provision that this commission may investigate trusts, mergers and the like.' If we pass the subsection in its present form we are placed in this peculiar position; *we have not less than three forums in this country authorized to investigate trusts, combines, mergers and _ the like. We have the proceeding prescribed by the Tariff Act which provides that an investigation into combines and mergers may be held before judges and these investigations may be held upon the recommendation, appointment, or order of the Governor in Council. I think it would appeal to any reasonable man that the proper forum for such an investigation would be before a judge or judges of the courts of this country. I think the whole House will agree with me that the judges from one end of Canada to the other are men in whom the public have every confidence and for whom the whole nation entertains the very highest regard and respect. I believe that we could all submit such a matter as this is to the judges with absolute confidence that their views will be unbiased by any feeling of partisanship or by any school of thought in regard to tariff, high tariff, low tariff, tariff for revenue or free trade, and that before the judges and perhaps before them only, you can have, from beginning to end, a fair, square inquiry that will go to the root of things and a fearless finding of results. I think that the section in the Tariff Act is broad enough to provide for this inquiry taking place as it should take place. My suggestion a day or two ago was that a reasonable amendment to that particular clause of the tariff law would suffice. Appoint some gentleman as counsel on behalf of the people or the government and make him the active agent of the government in the prosecution, or in the inquiry, or examination into the affairs of these mergers and combines. That is the forum which I would approve. But, there is another forum. Under the combines Act, I believe, it is provided that any five or seven persons-I think it is seven-may make application for an inquiry. There are two forums. Now comes this proposal for a third forum. Is a third forum necessary or essential? Is there any reason why Mr. GUTHEIE.
one or both of those now existing should not be used in preference to the third? The third forum is to be the Tariff Commission appointed by this government and I have no doubt in my mind that the hon. -member for St. Antoine, was quite fair, quite candid, quite accurate in hie statement as to the qualifications of the men who will sit on that board. I do not think he took advice from the members of the government when he made the statement but I have not heard any of them repudiate the statement and I am satisfied that he stated the fact when he said that the commission will be conservative and protectionist. The commissioners will have to be men in sympathy with the protectionist feelings of the present administration. Would you not rather have a board of judges?' Would it not be fairer to have a board of judges to inquire into this matter? There are so many mergers to-day that one is almost afraid to count them up or to imagine what the actual capitalization of these concerns is as apart from the watered capitalization. When one considers the effect which they may have, or which they have to-day, upon the great question that is agitating the public mind in regard to the cost of living one sees the necessity at once of going before the tribunal which is most likely to go into the question fearlessly and fairly and to reach a proper result, Would it-' be this board of tariff commissioners or would it be a board of independent judges in the courts of this country? I have no hesitation in saying, as I said before, that the mergers of Canada would laugh at your Tariff Commission. Give them a chance of selecting the forum to conduct this investigation and they will select the Tariff Commission and not the judges.
Something has been said about mergers -I do not know that I shall go into it now -perhaps at a future time I may have an opportunity-but there is this to be said that, notwithstanding the statement made last night by the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, who I believe, -said that if it could be demonstrated that the effect of the merger of the Ames-Holden and other companies had been to increase the cost of boots and shoes, the product of these factories, to the consumer, he would readily consent to have the 'present tariff wiped out.
No.
No, reduced 25 per cent.

Reduced. Well, I do not think it is necessary to prove that. My view of it is that with the over-capitalization of that and other companies and -prices are too hig-h to-day, it is not the question of increasing the price

or reducing the price to the consumer, who is the wearer of boots and shoes. It is so apparent on its face, that one hardly need state it in this House, or to make anything more than a passing remark with regard to it. Take a compamy-^I do not mean the Ames-Holden Company,-hut take any company in which there is an actual capital of $100,000 invested-that money has been paid into it-and the effect of these mergers that take place is to double, treble and multiply that capital, not by new money, but simply by the issue of new stock. A company with $100,000 invested in actual cash, may be recapitalized by the modern process into a company with $1,000,000 of bonds preferred stock, common stock and you see the result. In order to obtain five per cent, on the nominal capital, you have to earn $50,000 on the $100,000 that went into the business. You have to earn $50,000 on the actual investment in order to pay five per cent on the capitalization.
I suppose the hon. gentleman is quite aware that many of these companies pay no dividend whatever on their common stock and will not pay any dividend until the water has been entirely squeezed out.

I know there are all sorts of processes in connection with these schemes and I will admit that the hon. member from Montreal, St. Antoine, is more familiar with practices of this sort than I am. Perhaps the Minister of Finance will give us both pointers.
The only thing I object to is that this is criticised by men who know very little about it.

I am trying to give a few plain, blunt facts that appeal to me and it certainly appeals to me on the face of it, to be wrong in every sense of the word, to see the Aimes-Holden Company, or any other company into which a limited amount of capital has been placed, being capitalized up to two or three times that amount. That is a fraud on the face of it. While I do not know the various processes by which these ends are attained, I state plainly and bluntly that an investigation in regard to them should take place and while the Ames-Holden merger would very gladly submit their affairs to the Tariff Commission, they will be very reluctant to submit their affairs to a board of judges that were appointed under the Canadian Combines Act. [DOT]

Will the hon. member allow me to give him one piece of information, because I know he always tries to do what is just and fair in debate, and I have not had occasion hitherto to criticise him on that point. He repeatedly has referred to this company with which apparently I have the
misfortune to be connected, and I shall [DOT] make one statement for his benefit because it is a statement that will be applicable to the allegations made by other honourable gentlemen on that side of the House. My statement is:	Every dollar of the bonds
and preferred stock of the Ames-Holden-Me Cready Company represents actual money invested. So far as the common stock is concerned, there has never been a dollar of dividend paid upon it, nor is there expected to be a dividend paid upon it until that also represents actual assets.
Well, Mr. Chairman, so much for that clause-
Oh.

I know there are a great many gentlemen on the other side who applaud these mergers. I cannot find it in me to do it, and I know there are seated in this House many personal friends of my own who are very deeply interested in the question of mergers.

Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question? Does the hon. gentleman not remember that a year ago, the day before yesterday, a motion was made in this House to investigate such mergers, and the government that the hon. gentleman supported, and he himself amongst them, voted that motion down.
I do not remember the question to which my hon. friend refers.
I can tell you.
I say it is no part of the duty of parliament to investigate mergers; we have a law which provides a way in which they should be investigated and why not put that law in force now or at any time.
Why not put it in force then?
Who made the complaint?
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier.
What merger does my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) refer to?
I refer to the motion made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), now the Minister of Public Works.

I do not remember it at all. I do not know whether I was here, but even if I were here I probably would have voted against the motion because I have no doubt the motion was wrongly brought or it would not have been voted down by parliament. But, I find to-night, from the generous applause that greets the

question of mergers from the other side, that tihere is a tremendously strong feeling in their favour among the Conservative ranks in this House.
Oh.

Well, I have noticed the marked applause that greets the mergers from hon. gentlemen opposite. I heard the Minister of the Interior a few days ago make a distinct statement in regard to mergers, on the question of the cost of living. It was a very excellent statement. He said! that no question had given the government so imuch trouble or called for so much consideration from the government as that very question of mergers and the cost of living. I thought at the time that the Minister of the interior was serious, hut I do not know that he will make very much headway against mergers, trusts and combines with the present representation on the Conservative side of the House of Commons, because evidently there are only two questions brought before this House which they will applaud. One is: whenever the question of mergers is mentioned there is applause loudi and prolonged, and again, the only real cheer hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House can get out of them is when the sacred word 'protection' is used; 'protection ' cheers from the government side;
' high protection ' more cheers; and ' highest protection ' loud and prolonged cheers.
If my hon. friend will permit me-

I do not wish to be interrupted again. There have been occasions in this House, recently, when there was anything but a government cheer. We did not hear much united cheering from the government side when the Ne Temere was up; we did not hear any united cheer when the government's naval policy, or lack of naval policy, was before this House, hut you talk, of trusts and mergers, then my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) is cheered to the echo by his friends, when I am almost prevented from speaking because of interruption. When you talk of protection, or higher protection, or highest protection, then cheers from the government supporters ring throughout the walls of this Chamber. However, these remarks are a little beside the question and I 3hall get back to the clause. I now beg to move, seconded by Mr. Carvell:
That the words ' under the direction of the minister ' in line 2 of subsection 1 of section 4 of the Bill, be struck out.
Amendment (Mr. Guthrie) negatived, Yeas 40; Nays 76.
I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Carvell:

That the words ' to the minister ' in the last clause ' g ' of subsection 1 of section 4 be struck out and the words ' to parliament ' be substituted therefor.
Amendment (Mr. Guthrie) negatived.

I beg to move seconded by Mr. Carvell:
That subsection 3 of section 4 of the Bill be struck out.

Before that amendment is put I want to point out this phase of it. It is proposed now to put the trying of these mergers and combines practically out of the hands of the judges in whose hands it is at present.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not so proposed at all.

The object of this Bill, if it means anything, is that this commission shall be in a position to try such cases as have previously been tried by the judges. You appoint this commission for five years, and let us suppose that just before those five years are up, one of these combines ox mergers is complained of, and it goes before this commission for trial. This commission knows very well that the government is in favour of these combines and mergers, and is it likely to be in as good a position to try the case impartially 'as would be one of the judges of the Superior Courts? I think this clause ought to be struck out. We have already two tribunals before which these cases can be tried, and why appoint a third? To take the matter out of the hands of the judges and to put it in the hands of a partisan commission seems to me to be absolutely unfair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are responsible for the Bill, and not foT the hon. gentleman's understanding. There is nothing in the Bill that takes away the present power to have any such matter investigated by the judges. There is simply power to send it to this additional tribunal if so desired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But no
reason has yet been given why this second tribunal should be added to what we have already, or to show that it would be more in accordance with the public interest. Up to the present time we have had a law on the statue-book declaring that under certain circumstances an investigation, if it took place, should take place before a judge. Has any reason been given to show that the public interest would be better served or more justice done to the people at large if such an investigation took place before this commission? Although this is a new jurisdiction, I say it is not an improvement, but rather a deterioration. It is not possible to expect that mien who would he of the character stated by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames),

that is to say partisans, men in sympathy with the policy of the government, will do more substantial justice than men who are out of politics altogether. This is a very good reason why we should adhere to the present law and not adopt this amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have explained in the House, at least six times, that this tribunal, having practical knowledge and experience of such matters, is a very desirable tribunal to add to those already, appointed under the Customs Act. It does not seem to me that it would require a great deal of intelligence to understand that. The right Iron, gentleman asks questions about it. He might just as well ask, why did you add the judge of the Exchequer Court to the judges of the other courts ? The question would be just as relevant and just as intelligent. There is nothing taken away from tbe power to send an inquiry to any judge at the present time; but because a commission is to be established which will have knowledge and experience in these matters, we have thought it desirable to give power to send an inquiry to that tribunal if it should be thought best. Nothing is taken away. Additional power is granted to the government, which is responsible for these matters, and which will be responsible as to the tribunal to which they send them. That is all that is comprised in the suggestion that this commission shall be created as an additional tribunal; and there are other reasons which could be given.

My right hon. friend is trying to draw a herring across the path of this Bill when he intimates that anybody is suggesting that he is trying to take away from the judges the power to investigate these combines. Nobody has made such a suggestion. My right bon. friend knows that the judges have no poweT to investigate combines until he and his council ask them to do so, and he knows that he is providing a tribunal to which he can send these complaints instead of to the judges, and that is what we are finding fault with. I wonder if the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) would not rather have his boot and shoe merger investigated by a commission of good Conservatives well grounded in the principles -of protection, than to have it investigated by a non-partisan judge, who will render .a finding in accordance with the facts. I wonder whether there is a trust in Canada which would not rather have its case investigated by a partisan commission such as this Bill provides than by the judges of the land. There is no use in trying to cloud the object of this Bill from the members of this House or to make the country believe that we do not understand what we are talking about. We know exactly 96
the object of this Bill, and we are trying to make it plain. We know that the object of this Bill is to take, not tihe power, but the actual fact of the investigation of these combines away from the judges of the land, and place it in a partisan commission which will without doubt give the kind of answer the hon. gentleman wants when he sends it to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is most amazing to me that all the mergers, combines and trusts in Canada have sprung up since the 21st day of September last. If they existed before that date, why did not the late government take advantage of this clause in the Customs Act, and take steps to dissolve them? We have had a good deal of talk from hon. gentlemen opposite, but better evidence of their real opinion is offered by what they did or refrained from doing than by what they say. All the capitalizations that have been spoken of to-day existed prior to the 21st of September last, and did the late government take any action on their own initiative to investigate these combines for the purpose of ascertaining whether prices wrere unduly enhanced or not? I heard some one say something about a paper combine. After 15 years of power, that was the solitary instance of governmental action in regard to combines. All I have to say is that no matter what hon. gentlemen opposite may say to-day, they were not, when in power, on unfriendly terms with the trusts, mergers and combines of this country.
I say that their actions then do not correspond with their words now, and I prefer as between words and actions to rely upon their actions rather than upon their words, although I do not mean in any way to be offensive, because 1 understand this is a debate and they are trying to give an appearance to this Bill that it does not fairly bear. We have heard talk about almost everything in the Heavens above, and the earth beneath and the waters under the earth in reference to this Bill. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has traversed almost the known universe but has failed to debate this Bill on its merits and he knows it. I would do injustice to his intelligence if I believed that he was in his own judgment fairly interpreting that Bill this evening. He said that this Bill had been drafted without regard to the farming population. He is an intelligent man, and as I pointed out this afternoon in the interpretations clause here, which is taken from the Customs Act, the word ' products ' was deliberately added to the wording of the Customs Act in order that it might include the product of the farmer. I ask whether the word products does not include the products of the farmer. Is not ' agricultural products ' an every day



expression, is it not an ordinary use of the word ' product ' which, was put in expressly for the purpose of meeting the case of the farmer? I say that of all the people of Canada who will derive advantage from the information that will be collected by the Tariff Commission the farmers stand to benefit the most. Take the interpretation clause:
(d) ' Goods ' means products, wares and merchandise or movable effects of any kind, including, but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, horses, cattle and other animals.
Is there any merger or trust in horses, cattle and other animals? Are they not products of the farm? Do they not come within the provisions of this Bill and are not the farmers who raise these animat entitled to the benefit of the information which will be obtained by this commission? I would do injustice to the intelligence of the House if I assumed anything else.
Take subsection 4, in respect of the cost of production, and compare it with the interpretation clauses. It refers to the product of the farmer as well as of the manufacturer or of the company or combine, and the farmer is represented there. What do we wish to obtain? The cost of production in Canada as well as elsewhere for the farmer as well as for the manufacturer and merger. The cost, efficiency and conditions of labour in Canada and elsewhere in order that we will know what the farmer pays for his labour as compared with farmers in other countries. ' The prices received by the producers, merchants, &c. This clause includes farm products.
Is the minister going to fix the tariff on farm products on the basis of the prices paid by the farmer for the labour he uses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
1 say that labour enters into the price of the products of the farm just the same as of any commodity or the products of any factory in Canada, all conditions and factors which affect or enter into the cost of products. One of the great questions of the last campaign was the price of horses and cne advantage of the man on the plains over the Ontario farmer for the supplying of horses for northern Ontario. Is that not pertinent and important to the farmers who raise the horses? It is an absolute perversion to say that this Bill does not provide for the case of the farmer. This Bill meet3 the case of every class of people in Canada. It is designed to meet the cases of all the population of the country and it is an absolute perversion to read anyuung else into it.
My bon. friend this afternoon paid me the compliment of again saying that I Mr. WIDTH (Leeds).
was the representative of interests. Let me tell him that I am a representative of interests, I am here as the representative of the public interests, I represent the interests of the people of Canada, and while I am here I shall endeavour to discharge this trust and if the hon. member keeps as free from sinister influences as I do he will do well. I said before and I say now that I never have had and I have not now any connection with any trust, merger or combination, and I defy any man in Canada to prove that I have. Hon. gentlemen may find some fault with my capacity but I want them to understand
I never made any insinuation against the hon. gentleman.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He said from his place that I was the representative of the interests, of the trusts, mergers and combines.
I never made any insinuation against the hon. gentleman of having any interest in any trust, merger or combine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You said I represented the interests
And I adhere absolutely to that statement.
Take it back.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
