speechtext: I say I am not the representative of such interests, and that I am quite capable of discharging my duties m an impartial manner, and I think he might very well omit these suggestions although I take it from him that he has withdrawn anything in the nature of a personal allusion.
I never made any or wished to make any.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You said it.
Not personally, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To come down to the matter of this particular case with regard to the investigation of trusts, combines and mergers, as I have said, hon. gentlemen opposite lament that we are about to withdraw the privilege of submitting these cases to the courts. We are not withdrawing them, we are simply adding a tribunal. While hon. gentlemen speak in this way, yet in 15 years of power one single solitary instance is all that can be cited by hon. gentlemen opposite of their having recourse to the courts with regard to trusts, mergers and combines. They say it is a tremendous national loss that , the courts should be lost to them, and

yet to what extent did they use the courts? Let me state what my predecessor, a very able man, of whom I shall always speak with the greatest respect, said about trusts, mergers or combines:
In that shape the resolution passed the House, and is part of the tariff law to-day. While it imposed a check on the government, it had this disadvantage, that it provided a somewhat slow_ piece of machinery. Justice in the courts is somewhat slow; judges are busy, and men who thought there were combines, were slow to take advantage of the provision.
That answers my right hon. friend, it is from his righthand man, who said that justice is slow, and I add to that that justice is sometimes technical. We are not taking away from the court the hearing of these cases, not for a moment; we are adding a tribunal which can hold an inquiry in a very informal manner, which is not so bound by technical rules and which from the nature of the investigation into industrial conditions would be the best possible tribunal to inquire. That is all that we have in view in regard to this Bill. All this afternoon we have listened to iteration and reiteration as to keeping knowledge from parliament and yet if there is anything that has been made as plain as daylight, by every man who has spoken with responsibility, it is that parliament is to be entitled to all the information we may obtain. Nothing could be clearer than that.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had agreed in the view; that this information should go to parliament. So he did, but it was precisely in the same sense that the rest of us agreed, it must come to parliament because my hon. friend said in his trenchant and clear way that parliament was not disciplined and organized to take the initiative at all and if any one will consider for a moment the principle of responsible government, he must realize as a matter of fact that the government which has to take the initiative, must have the information given to it m order that it may take the initiative. It is the government that takes the initiative, that brings down its tariff Bill.
The very purpose of this legislation has been explained time and again in this debate. Over and over again it has been stated that the government wants to get information on which it may rely when it is considering the tariff law. Now, I said the other day that my hon. friends opposite were creating bogeys. I say so now. They are reading into this Bill what does not exist in the Bill, what never was intended to exist in the Bill, and what I think most of them know, does not exist and was not
96*
intended to exist in the Bill. But they wish to make things different from what they are-it is not what things are, but what they may be made to appear, that counts. These hon. gentlemen were so long in power that they grew skilled in that kind of thing. They have not lost this skill, and they are using it to-day to try I to give a false appearance to the Bill. The Bill is precisely what it purports to be, a means of obtaining information, a means which my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) endorsed in his speech before the manufacturers in Montreal, as I proved before. These hon. gentlemen are fighting bogeys which they themselves have raised. But all this will fail of effect when the work is in hand. It is measures and acts that count; and when the Tariff Commission is in action, my hon. friends will see that this is a beneficial measure. They will find it used for the best interests of the country. And, if it is not so used, the government is responsible, and the people will1 take care that a government is placed in power that will act in their interests through the Tariff Commission, and otherwise. That is the principle, and that principle has not been departed from in the least in connection with this Bill.

It seems to me a very significant circumstance that we have just heard from two ministers of the Crown, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White, Leeds). I am not naturally the best tempered of men myself; but I really cannot congratulate either of these ministers on the temper in which they have addressed the committee. My right hon. friend the leader of the government, whom I have always regarded with almost affection, referred to me and to other members on this side in terms that were hardly respectful. He said that 'any man of intelligence surely could see that.' The imputation was that nobody on this side of the House had intelligence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. He misunderstood me. I thought my hon. friends opposite did see it.

Yet the right hon. gentleman knew they did not see it, for they had so declared. The Minister of Finance has shown an amount of temper that is a perfect surprise to me. He ha' been wreathed in sweet smiles since he came to this House. That hon. gentleman also is a lovable personality. Yesterday, he was complaining that we were only engaged in a pillow fight. Well, when at boarding school, I had pillow fights, but I am bound to say that I never saw a boy in a pillow fight get into such a state of

temper as my hon. friend has shown. There was no need for temper, no need for defending his personal character, because there has been no imputation on his personal character.
Oh, oh.

That is a pretty general interruption, but it is somewhat inarticulate. If I were charged as a farmer in this House with acting in the interests of the farmers, I should not take it as a charge that I had a personal object to serve or that I was occupied by my own personal desire for gain, being personally tied up to the farming profession. A public man-and really one has to say these things, for after all is said and done, we are all public men here, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, who is a very young parliamentarian must not take every charge made against him in his public capacity as a charge upon his personal character. I venture to say that to the hon. gentleman; and I think if I had had the opportunity to speak some such words before he rose, he would not have got so angry. I do not know what the cause of anger is in this case. But I must say it makes me apprehensive. If it be the statement of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) well, that hon. gentleman always makes his statements emphatically. If it be that hon. gentleman's statements about trusts, mergers and combines that makes the Minister of Finance so angry I am apprehensive. For there is an old French proverb:	Qui s'excuse, s'accuse.
These hon. gentlemen are defending themselves with too much warmth on this subject of mergers for a western farmer to be quite comfortable. They make me fearful- not of their debate, because the man who loses his temper in debate is done-but fearful that there is a closer connection between the mergers and themselves, than they are willing to admit-I mean a public connection; the hon. gentleman must not be angry with me.
As to the amendment, the law as it is at present puts the initiative for examining these conditions into the hands of the people; that is my understanding of it. The anti-combines Bill enables any seven people to make an application to the Governor in Council for a court, and action is taken. The initiative is in the hands of the people, and that seems to me a very good thing. But I am afraid that the people are not going to get the consideration in these matters that they should have. I have explained in regard to the general matter my fears upon this question, and I have not heard in any of the subsequent parts of the debate anything which has cleared my mind of these fears. From the time of Magna Charta to the Lloyd George budget-
Oh, oh.

The interruptions are still somewhat inarticulate, Mr. Chairman. From the time I first mentioned until the other day-perhaps it suits my hon. friend better to have it put *that way; his knowledge of history may be a little limited-the British peciple, who, after all, have laid the foundation of free institutions and parliamentary governments the world over, have fought for the right of taxation as the inalienable right of parliament. They have been most jealous of any interference with that right. They cut off a king's head to take away from him the power to interfere with them in that matter. And in the next generation they drove a king from the throne, still fighting for the power of the people to tax themselves through parliament and the executive government. And the other day, in Great Britain, the House of Lords had taken from it forever the power of veto of an Act of the House of Commons and the power to interfere with a money Bill at all. I take it that this reference, being met with laughter or smiles in many parts of the other side of the House, is an indication of the hollowness of the (professions of hon. gentlemen opposite of affection for the mother country and its institutions. My attachment to those institutions cannot be questioned,-never has been questioned; my attachment to the flag has never been questioned. But I am bound to say that there are hon. members here who seem to regard these institutions in another light from that in which I regard them.
Now the initiative in this thing arises with the people. It has been contended that the Tariff Commission is meant to get the information. Analyse the taxing pow-er of the people a little further, and our information has been got to guide parliament and government in their taxing power. What is the constitution of Canada, as in the United Kingdom? It is that on a wider or narrower suffrage parliament is elected, and from that parliament an executive government is appointed. In Canada there is a little difference. We appoint our Cabinet ministers in a different w ay than in the old country, and I cannot think that the innovation is a good one. But that is the constitution in both countries. In various departments of the government you have the whole power of the people, for the time that you are in office, to make each of your departments as powerful as you want, them to be, to spend all the money you like, to get what information you like. That has been the method of government from time immemorial in every country that forms a portion of the British empire. Now why have the British people gone through with that fight? Because

the power of the purse resting in parliament is the only thing which guarantees the liberties of the people. We fought in the past against the despotism of kings, we fought until the other day against the unrestricted despotism of the House of Lords; and it is a sad thing to me that I come here to be subjected to another despotism, forsooth of the representatives of trusts and mergers. I must say that the tyrants of the past had some dignity about them. They had some tradition, but the conscienceless millionaires of this country have neither dignity nor anything else; they are guided by one consideration and that is the support and strengthening of their own interest at the expense of the general public.
Now what do you propose to do in this clause? Both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have said that you are not restricting that power, you are introducing a new power, it is an added power, and it.is the knowledge of British history and of what we have had to do to establish the power of parliament that makes me fear this additional power. The Anti-Combines Bill, I did not know that it was likely to do much. When it was discussed in this House in the last parliament I described it as a pill to cure an earthquake. A bludgeon is the only cure for the diseases that arise from a tariff, and so far as this went it was thoroughly constitutional. \\hat does the Minister of Finance say about this added power? I hope I am quoting him correctly. He says: 'The power we have added, we think, will be the best possible tribunal.' Why, that is an extraordinary confession, it is a confession which justifies everything that has been said on this side in support of my hon. friend's amendment. If it is the best possible tribunal, why is it so? It is not that in the light of history, it is not that in the light of establishing the taxing power of parliament, it is the best possible tribunal because it is the instrument of the government. I am afraid to utter the next sentence, but I do it without any personal reflection; it is the best possible tribunal and the best instrument of the government, because the government is, I fear, the instrument of another power, another despotism-care I say trusts? The word might make them angry. It is the best possible tribunal, I repeat, because it is a tribunal which the government themselves are creating, it is their instrument, and I very much fear that they are using the forms of the old constitutions of this country, and of Britain, to put a buffer between themselves and the people, to put a buffer between themselves and their responsibility. That
is why I most heartily support this amendment.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance said that actions count Well, I admit it. But after all, in discussing parliamentary measures we have to talk some. I remember an instance in British history of a great statesman who held the position of Chancellor of the Exchequer, a position analogous to that held by my hon. friend the Finance Minister. That statesman was William Pitt, he got there in a year and a half, and he got there by means of three speeches which at once marked him out as the most brilliant parliamentarian that had been seen in England for a century. So he went on and proved himself to be. I must say, for a man who discards any belief in words, as my hon. friend did, he is a pretty good talker himself. He speaks extremely well, and frequently. If he goes on as fast as he has since he came to the House, we will be able to remind him of his saying that it is actions that count and words are nothing. I told my hon. friend yesterday that I feel an interest in him, I ventured to describe him with the best of good temper as a man who had entered upon a rake's progress. I hope I was thoroughly wrong, and that his political history will turn him out as a man who will restrain those men behind him who are at present cheering protection to the echo. But I have my fears. However, I am here as a representative of the western farmers-who have no interest in this commission, of course. The real fact is that you cannot protect the farmers of this country, the great bulk of the farmers, for the simple reason that they produce far more than they can use, and have to send the overplus abroad. No protection to them is possible, that is why they are excluded from the operation of this Bill.
As a representative of the western farmers I can only say that I take the statement of my hon. friend that actions count as equal to an assurance of good conduct on his part. I take it as almost equal to an assurance that he will show us-I do not say in his next budget because he has not got his commission into working order yet-but in the budgets of this parliament some real and substantial reductions of taxation. I hug that hope to my heart and I need some soothing of my alarms because I am very much afraid tliat the result of this measure will be the raising of the tariff and not the lowering of it. In the meantime I will get such consolation as I can from the assurance of my hon. friend. I have very great pleasure in supporting this amendment.

One would hardly be human if he did not feel stirred by the outrageous abuse which has been hurled from the other side for many hours past at all men who may be considered as at all

connected with the manufacturing industries of Canada. I do not wish to pursue the argument in the vein in which hon. gentlemen opposite have pursued it but all I can say to them is that they are barking up the wrong tree in my judgment and that no party will stay long in power that attempts to pull down that which during the last thirty years has been built up-the vast industries of Canada. I want to tell these hon. gentlemen-and I have specially in my mind the two hon. gentlemen who are sitting on the second bench, the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, Mr. Clark (Red Deer) and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie)-that they are not speaking for the people of Canada today. They say that the manufacturers number two or three thousand and that all this is for their benefit. These manufacturers are employing about 500,000 workmen who are dependent upon the manufacturers for their daily bread and they are just as much entitled to respect and to honour as are the farmers of Red Deer. I want to say to the hon. member for Red Deer-I have not had an opportunity of speaking with him before-that he is not speaking for the whole people of England to-night. I know a little about England as well as he does. I have taken part in two campaigns in England and I want to tell him that half the people in England are against his economic principles. I want to tell him that there is a greater chance of protection being introduced into Great Britain than there is of the policy of free trade being introduced into Canada. There is no doubt that the hon. gentleman has free trade at heart, but there is a doubt whether he understands the people of Canada to-day. We have been engaged for thirty years in building up this nation. We have employed in the factories to-day 500,000 workingmen. There are only 700,000 upon farms with 900,000 workers of all kinds who are not upon farms. Do not run away with the idea that this is a purely agricultural country and that every other industry must hide its head because the farmer says so or because those who profess to represent the farmers say so. The hon. gentleman has just told us that the farmer cannot be protected. Let me refer him to the pages of the Ottawa papers last week which quoted potatoes at $2.50 a bag. Is not that a fit subject to be investigated by the Tariff Commission? What is the cost of producing potatoes in Canada? Is it any thing like $2.50 a bag? The workmen have to pay that price and they pay it uncomplainingly. I take the ground that we are going to be a united people from end to end, a people who will give and take and this cry of mergers combines and so on is not going to down long tire people of Canada. These gentlemen Mr. COCKSHTJTT.
sat for fifteen years with these mergers and combines at their back and they did not make the least effort to put them down. But, as soon as they begin to pull down the industries of this country, they, will find that the farmer of Canada will suffer along with other citizens. We are all bound together in one common interest, and I say to these gentlemen who would endeavour to strike at the manufacturers because he only represents two or three thousand people, that when they hit at the manufacturer they hit at every man who is working for him, and I am proud to-day that the workmen of Canada are much more contented and much happier than are the workmen of the country from which the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Clark) comes. Let him explain what is the matter in Great Britain to-day, when every great industry is threatened with strikes. What about the coal strikers who have voted by four to one to go on strike? What is that for? The hon. gentleman has given us no reason, and he cannot say that free trade has banished all industrial and economic ills. They have tried all kinds of quack nostrums in England under Lloyd George to cure the evils by which they were oppressed-their pension Bills, their old, worn-out insurance against unemployment, and that sort of thing-everything but giving an honest day's wage for an honest day's labour. The first right of a citizen is the chance to have an honest day's pay for an honest day's labour. Still, we have this hon. gentleman coming out from England to tell us that for thirty years we have been on the wrong track, that we do not know how our people are being wronged by tariffs, and taxes, and mergers and combines. These words flow glibly from the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), the hon. member from South Wellington and others. The people of Canada are being well served by the manufacturers and the workman, and with all this howl about the farmer we have not heard one single word in the debate about the interests of the working men. They are struggling just as hard as the farmers. They have just as much right to live, and I believe that when the people of Canada look this question over they will tell these men that they are wrong. They will tell the hon. member for South Wellington, at least the people of Guelph will, if I know them, that he is not preaching sound doctrine. I do not wonder that my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) drew the line at allowing them a trip hammer the other day when they wanted one brought in without paying duty. There is a trip hammer there now and the Minister of Customs did not want another to get in without paying duty, and therefore my hon .friend will have to

pay the duty, and rightly so. If the manufacturers in other centres have to pay duty on trip hammers, why should my hon. friend be permitted to bring his trip hammer in free? What I ask the hon. member for South Wellington, the hon. member for Red Deer and the people of Canada to do is to look this question in the face. This measure has 'been brought down to better conditions. I am not prepared to say whether, in its working out, it is going to do all the things that are expected, but it means the searching for information, and if information is going to make any difficulty, it is the first time I have known it to make difficulty. The information that is to be searched for is to enable us to have a scientific tariff. Unlike free trade, a protective tariff is a science, not a fixed science, but an applied science, and the beauty of the tariff is that you can apply it to the conditions. Then the hon. member for Red Deer said that goods ought to be brought in more freely because the revenue is too high. That will produce more revenue. A reduction in the tariff has been known in times past to produce more revenue, and it may do so again. Why reduce the tariff if you want to reduce the revenue? Increase the tariff and stop imports, stop the hundred million dollars excess that is spent on imports from going out of this country to the other nations of the world and keep money in our own pockets. It is not as the hon. member for Red Deer or as the hon. member for South Wellington says, oversea commerce that counts-not by a long way.
To-day the test of a nation's success is tlm degree of efficiency and economy with which it can supply its own wants. Compare the United States, that great protectionist country, with Great Britain, that great free trade country, if you can call her so, and I say that the condition of the workingman and o.f the farmer in the United States is far superior to that of the corresponding classes in Great Britain. The hon, member for Red1 Deer (Mr. Clark) may question that, but I can point to the report of a commission which recently came from England to investigate the conditions in the United States, and which on its return sets forth that the workingman of the United States, with all your high cost of living, and your high tariff, is better off than the workingman in so-called free trade England. I tell the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that there is a great probability that in the near future, we will see a tariff for protection in the British Isles, land that no longer will it be pointed out that there is one great .free trade nation, and, equally true there is not likely to be any more. For fifty years free trade has been tried and
found wanting all along the line. If you take Great Britain as a sample of free trade, you will find if you look at her taxation, that She raises millions of dollars on tea and coffee and many other such things that are regarded as absolute necessaries of life, and which are staple articles of consumption by the 'workingman. L'et me ask the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), and I hope he wall be honest enough to admit it, what -class in Great -Britain to-day is anxiously demanding tariff reform; who cry the loudest in Great Britain for protection? Is it not the agricultural classes that are demanding tariff reform? I tell my hon. friend (Mr. "Clark) that tariff reform in the old land is coming without doubt, and that when it does come Great Britain will see an era of prosperity such as she never witnessed before. I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite to now let this Bill go through, they have fought it for hours and hours and it is time for them to cease vain argument. These gentlemen opposite tell us that this Bill is for the manufacturers only, but we have not asked for it as manufacturers. 1 am glad to know that undeT this Bill the 'cost of living will be investigated, because if potatoes are sold at two and a half dollars a bag when they should be sold for one dollar or one dollar and twenty-five cents, the workingman may have a remedy; if eggs are selling too high at fifty cents a dozen, and if wheat, oats, -and barley are sold at too high -a price, there may be a drop, and so we will see to it in the cities that if you get after the workingman we will know what is the matter with the farmer also that he does not produce at a lower price than he now sells for. I tell hon. gentleman opposite that the whole thing is a question of live and let live. I would advise hon. gentlemen opposite to cease their denunciation of the manufacturers and the workingmen of Canada; I would advise them to let this Bill go into force, and then, if they have any complaint against it, I am sure it will not be found in the measure itself but in the working of it. I believe here will never be any fault to be found with this measure if the men who are appointed as commissioners are the right kind of men. The member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) shed big tears because no room could be found on that commission for a free trader. Certainly not; my view is that the man who goes on a board to handle tariffs must be a man who believes that tariffs must be handled.
My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) says that a bludgeon is the only thing that ought to be used on a tariff and my answer to him is that the man who sets out to handle tariffs, must be a believer in tariffs, and must not be a man who- would use a bludgeon on tariffs. I

would ask the Minister of Militia if, when he is going to arm the militia of Canada, he would select Andrew Carnegie or the Kev. J. A. MacDonald to select a fit and proper rifle to put into the hands o-f the defenders of our country. Surely not, because they believe in complete disarmament, and they would pick out a gun that would not go off. And, that is exactly what would happen if you put men of the calibre of the hon. member for Eed Deer (Mr. Clark) on a Tariff Commission; you would be arming the commission with a gun that would not go off, and that is exactly what we don't want to do. There is no chance of the Minister of Militia asking the Peace Society to step in and pick out weapons with which to fight our enemies, and there is no chance of anybody who would use a bludgeon on the tariff being able to decide as to what is a proiper tariff for this country. I would appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite to let the Bill now go through, and let the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) think overnight on it before he moves any further amendments.

I am sure the House, during the time I have had the honour of sitting in it, has not had to complain of my occupying on the whole, more than my share of its time, and I ask for an opportunity to utter what I hope will be a few goodnatured sentences in answer to such direct appeals as have come to me from my hon. friend (Mr. Cock-shutt). I might tell the House, if I wanted to be critical or to get angry, that I found the speeches of my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) very useful campaign literature when 1 first fought for a seat in this House in 1908. I had recourse to ' Hansard ' and I found on the whole no more useful speeches to me for securing my seat in the House of Commons than the speeches of my hon. friend. Now that I have heard him, I can understand that. I appeal to the right hon. the leader of the House to say that there has been no undue delay in the discussion of this measure. We must admit that this legislation its in the nature of an innovation; it is a new thing; it is a very large measure, and I do not think the time that has been spent over it has been unduly long as yet. I should be the last man to countenance in any way any form of Parliamentary obstruction. I know the tight we had against it years ago, in the mother of parliaments, and I should be the last to counsel it. But, I contend, there has been no need for such an impassioned appeal as I have just heard from my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) for the immediate settlement of this question. That impassioned appeal reminds me that I will need a large stock of soothing syrup, if I have first to admin-Mr. COCKSHUTT.
ister it to the members of the Cabinet and then to take up private members afterwards. When my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) began in so stormy a tone, I thought we were getting from bad to worse, and really my duties in the way of soothing hon. members opposite will soon come to be very onerous indeed. I want to say to my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) that there is no man in Canada who wants to set class against class less than I do. I am a farmer; he is a manufacturer. I had explained in the few remarks I made to the House that, as a farmer, I make my living without protection. I have no protection. It is economically impossible for you to give it to me. I produce, or help to produce, more of the material of the farm than is needed in Canada, and I cannot be protected. I have got to sell every year what I produce; every thing that is ready for the market must go.
The manufacturer is in a different position. But the only point I want to put to my hon. friend is that I am protected, and I ask him, if he be so strong a man as his voice would indicate, to put himself alongside of the feeble Briton that he sees before him and live without government pap. Of course, I am under no illusions as to the early arrival of free trade in Canada; I know too much about fisealities to expect anything of the kind. I have argued again and again that the benefit of the western farmer is the benefit of the whole of Canada, and I honestly believe that what I am supporting is good for the whole of Canada and not simply for any class of the community. My life-long connection with the British Liberal party is a guarantee that I stand for the^ masses, and not for minorities of any kind, and my whole argument in this House will support me in that modest claim. I do not know whether my hon. friend was present when I spoke last night, or whether, if he was not present, he did me the honour of reading what I said.
I read it.

It has not had a very good effect up to the present. If he read it at all carefully, he would have found one statement which after all was an emphatic contradiction of something he has just said. He said he had not heard anybody mention the consumers in the country.
I said the workingmen.

Does the working man not consume? I have known a number of workingmen who had excellent appetites. I tried to make my argument clear that the consumers included everybody in the country. I would be loath to go into a discussion as to the com-
3041	FEBRUARY 13, 1912	3042
parative merits of the old country and Canada. A great many of us in this House love and respect both lands, and I do not think an acrimonious comparison of the two countries would be a good way to promote the sane imperialism in which we all believe. I would like to say in conclusion that I have never, in private or in public, said one word against Canada which was not justifiable criticism; but in parliament, as on the platform, we must discuss measures for the public good of the country in which we live, and it is only in that spirit that I criticise. If I did not do that, I would not be doing my duty to my constituents.

For the first time in this House we have a manufacturer proclaiming himself to be a great friend of the workman. He has not been a great friend of the workman all his life, if I am well informed. As he has said, there are about 500,000 workmen in the different industries of the country, and as he has brought the question before the House, I am in duty bound to say a few words in support of the workmen of the country. We have heard a great deal about a scientific tariff. I believe the 500,000 workmen that the hon. gentleman has mentioned regard that scientific tariff as a one-sided affair, because it is entirely in favour of the great manufacturers of the country. Protection, if I understand it aright, has the object of preventing goods from another country coming to this country without paying a heavy tax; that is for the benefit of the manufacturer. But what about the labour to manufacture those goods? Is there any protection for that labour? My hon. friend from Brantford knows that there is not. If there is no protection for labour, 1 claim that the tariff is a one-sided affair. In this House, and elsewhere, I have often heard men rise and say what good friends they were of the labour classes. In Brockville at the present time we find law-abiding Canadian citizens put out of work and strangers from the other side of the line puit in their places.
Is there not an alien labour law that protects the labourer?

I will cite to my hon. friend a case which was before the Montreal courts. The manufacturer, who was the Canada Car Company, stated that they could not get eoanpetenlt men in Montreal, which was untrue, but the presiding judge said that that statement by the manufacturer was enough, and we lost our case. There is the kind of protection we have, and it is a one-sided protection. My hon. friend is not satisfied with the expression ' trusts and mergers.' It is not my intention at present to discuss this question in detail, because I hope to do so in the near future. We talk about legislation, but if we were spending one-fourth of the time of this House to make legislation and three-fourths of the time to see it carried out, we would be doing better for tihe country. We are passing one piece of legislation after another, because I understand that this is an addition to existing legislation, and then we will probably have another piece added to it, to make it so that nobody can understand it.
My hon. friend f-om Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt) has no right to say that the working people of this country are satisfied, and the very remedy for tariff evils, the very remedy against the trusts and mergers, was presented before the people last year, on the 21st of September. Whether it was .carried or not makes no difference; it was presented, and if it had been presented and left bare as it should have been, without any waving of the flag or cries of all sorts, in fact if you were to take a referendum on that question alone to-day, I am convinced that a strong majority would pronounce in favour of that measure. I declare that nobody has the right to say the working people are satisfied. My hon. friend knows that very well, and if he had not said what he said to-night it was not my intention to take part in this discussion. 1 am not discussing the Bill, I am not a law maker, God forbid me from being a law maker of that kind. I am here representing the very finest division in the Dominion of Canada and the largest one. I have any number of manufacturers in my riding and it is not their fault that I now sit in this House. I claim that you can send your Tariff Commission all over Canada and abroad to make investigations a3 to the conditions of manufacture, but most of the information desired is now to be obtained in the Labour Department. The government will find there informa-*tion on the hours of labour, on the wages paid in different industries, on the wholesale and retail prices of goods. If it is desired to obtain information on the value of the plant of a manufacturer, will they be able to determine whether the manufacturer is overrating his plant? The fact that practically all the manufacturers and the mergers and combines were wholly against the measure submitted to the people in September last, is enough to show that that measure was in favour of the people. The hon. member speaks about potatoes at $2.50 a bag. What about butter at 40 cents a pound that was bought at 25 cents and put in cold storage until the merger raised the price to 40 cents? You can go to Ottawa stores and buy eggs

at 50 cents, out of cold storage. One grocer told me to-day that he had to sell the fresh eggs at the same price because the people could not afford to pay more. Does the farmer derive any benefit from the butter which he sells at 25 cents and which is retailed at 40 cents out of cold storage or from the eggs which he sells at 15 cents or 16 cents a dozen, which are now being sold at 40 cents? Where is the profit of the farmer in that? What about the third party in that case, the man who is responsible for the enhanced price? We don't seem to touch him at all.
I claim that this is done through the mergers! and the trusts and when the time comes I shall produce figures to show that we have 30 or 40 mergers and to prove their over-capitalization. I do not want a commission to find out the cost of living, I go from store to store and I have found exactly the real conditions of the cost of living in Montreal and Toronto, I will compare that with the cost in the United States and then we will have something to show to the members of the House the effect of the merger whether that merger has a right to exist, and whether the investigation thait we are now going to make into mergers will be beneficial to the masses or not.

I have been astonished that any opposition to this Bill is received with great surprise by hon. gentlemen opposite, and that they have not exhibited the best of temper in replying to any objections urged against it. Supporters of the government speak of this measure as if it were of divine origin, as if it was perfect land not Oipen to criticism and amendment. The motion before the House is that clause 3 be struck out. The right hon. gentleman who leads the House stated in reply to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that the reason for subsection 3 of section 4 being in this Bill had been explained three or four times, but he did not give a single reason for its existence in the Bill. Nor did the Minister of Finance give any reason for the presence of that particular clause. The House is entitled to some logical reason for the existence of this clause in the Bill. The purpose of the clause is to empower the Governor in Council to authorize the holding of an inquiry by the proposed Tariff Commission under section 12 of the Customs Tariff Act.
Under section 12 of the Customs Tariff Act the Governor in Council was empowered whenever it deemed it to be in the public interest to inquire into any conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement alleged to exist among the manufacturers to unduly promote the advantage of the manu-Mr. VERVILLE.
facturers or dealers in any article at the expense of the consumer. That clause of the Tariff Act empowered the Governor in Council to direct an investigation by certain judges.
If the judges reported that there was a conspiracy, the government had the power to remove the tariff upon uae particular article. I would point out that a conspiracy in restraint of trade, a condition of things such as was contemplated under section 12 of the Customs Tariff Act, is a violation of the criminal law of this country. And the party guilty of any violation of that part of the criminal law is liable to a penalty of $4,000 as a maximum, and $200 as a minimum, or two years imprisonment. I contend it is quite clear that an investigation of this kind should take place before judges of a court, parties competent to make an investigation.
It may be said that under section 12 of the Customs Tariff Act, the penalty is not the one described in the Criminal Code. But, if the judges report that there has been a violation of the law, that a conspiracy exists, it becomes the duty of the Crown to prosecute the conspirators criminally. This is a serious matter and those powers should not be delegated to the members of this commission. We do not know wno they may be. They may not be members of the legal profession, or qualified to take evidence under oath or to reach true findings on the evidence. I am not trying to delay the course of the Bill, but I submit that there is fair room for a debate about this section, and the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance should not treat it in the way they do. The whole question is: Shall the commission have power to conduct inquiries or shall tney not? The hon. member for South Weiiing-ton (Mr. Guthrie) urged that the clause be struck out and that the power of investigate! be left as at present under section 12 of the Customs Tariff Act. I submit that in aii fairness, the amendment of the hon. member is a reasonable one and I think it sliouid be supported by the committee, at least until some reason is given stronger than arj we have heard from members of the government in support of the clause as it stursas.

It seems to me that this i-s a matter of really (more importance than the Minister of Finance thinks it is. I was entirely unable to understand the reason why he objected so strongly to our criticism of this section and to our support of the amendment of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). I think it much against the proper administration of the law to have two or more different tribunals to try out the same matter. As has been pointed out we have a provision in the

customs law that reference may be made to a judge of the Exchequer court, or the Superior court or of the County court, and if such judge finds that there is conspiracy under which prices have been unduly increased the Governor in Council may reduce or abolish the duty. We have also the very excellent provision of the Combines Investigation Act. Section 1 of that Act makes provision almost in the same words as section 12 of the Customs Act that where, as the result of the investigation that is provided for, it appears to the satis-fection of the Governor in Council that there is a combine to unduly enhance prices, the Governor in Council may reduce or abolish the duty on the article.
That is a statute which may be invoked by the people-any seven residents of Canada may invoke it-and investigation takes place before a judge of one of the courts of the land. The Minister of Finance proposes that an investigation of a matter of this kind may be taken out of the hands of the people, or a iportion of the people, and handed over to the commission to be appointed under this Act. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) seemed to get very excited and urged that we were fighting the manufacturers, because we were supporting this amendment. What is the fair inference from the hon. gentleman's position? It is that he thinks that a tribunal like a judge of the Exchequer court or of the Supreme court will not be as favourable to 'the .manufacturers as the commission which the government is to appoint under this law. And I have no doubt that there might be cases when such an investigation would not be so favourable td a combine as would be the judgment of this Tariff Commission. Surely the Minister of Finance must see how objectionable it is to have two tribunals with authority to inquire into the same matter. The hon. gentleman has provided what _ may be in the nature of an appeal, giving the Governor in Council power to take the matter out of the hands of the tribunal. This may lead to endless confusion. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman should show some reason why the courts cannot be trusted to make these investigations. It is only within the last two or three years that combines and mergers have existed to any large extent in Canada. These organizations create a new situation in the country. We know that under the late government, after the Combines Act was brought into force, an investigation of the United Shoe Machinery company was undertaken at the instance of a number of 'people, who complied with the law. That matter is going on to-day; I believe the Minister of Labour took it up where it was left by his predecessor. Everybody admits that the Combines Act is an admirable law, well calculated to inquire
into these combines. That law is being tested. Nobody finds fault with it. We should not form another tribunal to take up cases which are already provided for.
Why should parliament be asked to ignore the tribunal which the law now provides, and give the Governor in Council authority to refer these cases to a tribunal which, from the very nature of its appointments, will be favourable to the manufacturers, to the producers, to the dealers, and. against the interests of the consumers? I fail to see any reason whatever for this Bill. We ought not to enact a law simply for the fun of the thing, we ought to have clearly shown to us that some evil now exists, and that there is a prime need for additional legislation on the subject. The government has wholly failed to present any reasons to the committee why this section should be adopted. Therefore, I am in favour of the amendment of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie).

I have listened with much interest to the discussion on this Bill. I must say that, although I have been in the House for five or six years, I never saw so much time lost over a Bill a3 over this. The Bill certainly points in the right direction. The Dominion canners have been mentioned as robbers and thieves. It is a strange thing to say, that we got our charter from a Liberal government and we operated under a Liberal government ten years. During all that ten years I never heard any fault found with the Dominion canners until this Bill was brought forward, and now we are styled as robbers. I want to say that the Dominion canners are doing a great business in this country, we are giving employment to about 9,500 people. We are also furnishing a market for the products of our soil, many thousand acres. Hon. gentlemen opposite are entirely wrong in what they have said against our industry. If you compare our prices with the American prices you will find that ours are much lower, our goods are better goods. Owing to the condition of the labour market, it is impossible for us to put up goods as cheaply .as they were put up a few years ago. We are paying the farmers ten or twelve per ton more for peas than we were a few years ago, for the reason that they have to pay more for their help. It is this great northwest we have heard so much about that has taken away the help from our farmers, and we can scarcely get sufficient labour to harvest our crop.
They are the people who buy your oanned stuff.

Very true, and we are glad to sell it to them, and we aTe selling it to them at a reasonable price. The hon.

member for Regina (Mr. Martin) the other day said that we had raised the price of tomatoes to $1.75 a case. The committee will be surprised when I tell them that the manners sold their tomato pack last year for less than $1 a dozen. After the goods leave our hands we have no further control over the prices. We do not *control the whole packing business. There are thirty or forty other canneries in the Dominion with which our company has to compete. I am strongly in sympathy with this Bill, because I think it will do justice to all. I am astonished at some of the arguments I hear from the opposition, they seem to me very unreasonable. Speaking for my own company, I am altogether in sympathy with the Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 4 be adopted?

I had an amendment that I wished to propose to section 4. If I may have an opportunity of bringing it up at a later stage, I would have no objection to allowing the section to pass at the present time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Carried.
On section 5,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think the time has come to adjourn.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have had a great deal of discussion, and have made very little progress. If we are ever to get through the session we will have to get along faster than we have done. I would like to sit here for an hour or two longer and get something done, if it will be convenient for hon. gentlemen opposite.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the discussion has been perfectly legitimate, at least on out side* there has been no intention of delaying the progress of the Bill. It is now one o'clock, and I think we should adjourn.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The discussion may have been legitimate, I am not saying that it was not. All I complain of is that the greater part of it has been repeated ten or fifteen times.
Does that remark apply to both sides?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It applies to any gentleman who happens to have been guilty of it; I am not discriminating.
It does not apply to me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend is anxious that we should adjourn now, I will agree to it. But I want to say distinctly that if we are going to discuss matters in that fashion, we will have to sit Mr. MARSHALL.
later, or else the session will have to be prolonged, and I do not think any one wants to prolong the session.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Nobody wants to prolong the session. But we have seen sessions lasting five or six months, and I think the hon. gentleman and his friends have contributed to prolong them. There has been no obstruction of this measure, only legitimate discussion. Our arguments may not impress the right hon. gentleman, and I am sorry for it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not finding fault with the quality of the arguments, except so far as they may be controverted. But I do find fault with unreasonable repetitions. It is not only waste of time, but it is wearisome.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I know it is wearisome, but I have been listening to just such arguments for fifteen years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no way of preventing it. The only result will be that we will have to sit a little later, or else have a longer session. I know we are all anxious to bring the session to a close at a reasonable date. The other alternative seems to be the only one, namely, that we must sit later. At the request of my hon. friend, I will move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, but with the understanding that if we are going to take so long with every one of the sections of this Bill, we must sit a good deal later.
Progress reported.
Mr. BORDEN moved the adjournment of the House.

I would like to give notice to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) that on the first convenient occasion upon going into Committee of Supply I wish to bring up the question of freight rates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What will be
the business of the House to-morrow?

My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) will probably go on with his estimates.
